I.01 Monolithic Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA One deployable unit containing UI, business logic and data access, sharing a single process and usually a single database. Keep everything in one codebase and one runtime so calls are in-process method calls and transactions are local ACID. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Distributed-system overhead (network calls, partial failure, versioning) for teams and products that do not need independent scaling. It is the default shape of early enterprise software; microservices emerged later to relieve its scaling and team-coordination limits. Single deployable — everything runs in one process How it works A request reaches the single application over HTTP. The web layer routes to the relevant module in the same process. Modules call each other through plain method calls. Data changes happen inside one local database transaction. The response returns; the whole artifact is built, tested and deployed together. Scaling is done by running N identical copies behind a load balancer. MONOLITHIC ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Simple to build, debug, test end-to-end and deploy. + Local ACID transactions; no distributed consistency Whole app scales and deploys as one unit; a defect can take it all down. problems. + Lowest latency for inter-module calls and low infra Coupling erodes boundaries over time without strict discipline. cost. Build and test times grow; large teams collide in one + One codebase makes refactoring across modules codebase. straightforward. Technology choices (language, framework) are locked in. When to use When not to use Early-stage products, small teams, well-understood domains, internal tools, and any system whose scaling profile is uniform and moderate. Many autonomous teams shipping independently, parts of the system with very different scaling or availability needs, or hard fault-isolation requirements. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Internal admin and back-office applications early-stage SaaS MVPs Line-of-business ERP modules Content sites on a single framework. Enforce internal module boundaries (packages, ArchUnit tests) to keep a later split possible. Run stateless instances behind a load balancer and scale the database vertically first. Keep a fast CI pipeline; use feature flags so deploy size does not equal release risk. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Simplicity, one deployable SCALABILITY Medium — horizontal clones, shared DB limit COUPLING High — internal MAIN DRAWBACK One failure/scale/deploy unit COMPLEXITY Low MAINTAINABILITY Medium — high initially, degrades with size BEST USE CASE Small teams, MVPs, uniform workloads ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

I.02 Layered Architecture (N-Tier) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Code organized into horizontal layers (presentation, application/business, persistence, database), each depending only on the layer below. Separate concerns by technical responsibility and constrain dependencies to flow downward. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Tangled UI, business and data-access code that is hard to test and change independently. Popularized by enterprise Java/.NET systems to give large teams a shared, predictable structure. Layers with strictly downward dependencies Client Service / component Database / store Sync call Dependency direction How it works A request enters the presentation layer, which validates and maps it. The presentation layer calls the business layer; it never calls persistence directly. Business rules run and coordinate one or more repositories. The persistence layer translates calls into queries. Results travel back up, mapped to DTOs at each boundary. “Closed” layers force requests through each tier; “open” layers may be skipped. LAYERED ARCHITECTURE (N-TIER) Advantages Disadvantages Familiar structure; easy onboarding and clear ownership. Business logic often depends on persistence design (anemic domain). Layers can be tested in isolation with mocks. + Swapping the UI or persistence technology is “Sinkhole” anti-pattern: requests pass through layers doing nothing. localized. A feature change touches every layer. Works well with frameworks like Spring MVC. Layer-based packaging hides business capabilities. When to use When not to use CRUD-heavy business applications, teams that want a conventional structure, and systems where the domain logic is moderate. Rich, evolving domains (prefer Clean/Hexagonal/DDD) and systems where features cut across layers constantly (prefer vertical slices). Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spring Boot REST backends with controller–service– repository packages Enterprise portals Decide per layer whether it is open or closed. Keep DTO/entity mapping at boundaries. Package by feature inside layers to avoid a technical-only view. Add ArchUnit rules to forbid upward dependencies. Banking back-office apps. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Separation by technical concern SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium — layer to layer MAIN DRAWBACK Business logic leaks into persistence COMPLEXITY Low MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Conventional business CRUD apps ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

I.03 Three-Tier Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A physical/runtime split into presentation tier, application tier and data tier, each deployed on separate infrastructure. Place UI, business logic and data on separately deployable and scalable tiers connected over the network. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Two-tier designs where clients held business logic and talked directly to the database, hurting security and scalability. Web applications needed thin clients, a protected data tier and the ability to scale the middle tier on its own. Three physical tiers across network zones Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works The browser loads static assets from the web/CDN tier. API calls go to a load balancer in front of the application tier. Any stateless app server handles the request. App servers are the only components allowed to reach the data tier. The database tier is replicated and backed up independently. Each tier is scaled and secured (firewalls, subnets) on its own. THREE-TIER ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Clear security zones; the database is never exposed to clients. Network hops add latency between tiers. The data tier remains a shared scaling bottleneck. + The application tier scales horizontally. Still one application codebase: coupling inside the + Tiers can be upgraded and operated independently. app tier. + Well understood by operations teams. More infrastructure to run than a single server. When to use When not to use Public-facing web applications needing network segmentation, horizontal app scaling and a protected database. Tiny apps where one server suffices, or systems that need per-capability scaling (move to services). Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Classic web shops on VMs Government citizen portals Keep the app tier stateless (externalize sessions to Redis). Put the DB in a private subnet. Use connection pooling and read replicas to relieve the data tier. Intranet HR systems. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Physical separation of presentation, logic, data COMPLEXITY Low–Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Secure, scalable web apps MAIN DRAWBACK Data tier remains a bottleneck ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment topology

I.04 Client-Server Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Clients initiate requests; servers own resources and logic and respond. The relationship is asymmetric. Centralize data and rules on servers, keep clients thin or specialized, and communicate through a request– response protocol. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Duplicated logic and inconsistent data across standalone programs; enables shared state and central control. Networking and shared databases made centralized service providers practical; it underlies almost every modern network application. Many clients, one server tier Client Service / component Database / store Sync call How it works A client opens a connection and sends a request. The server authenticates and authorizes the caller. The server executes logic against its data store. The server returns a response (data, status, errors). The client renders or acts on the response. State lives on the server; clients can be replaced freely. CLIENT-SERVER ARCHITECTURE Advantages Central data, security and rules; one place to update. Heterogeneous clients share one backend. Simple mental model and tooling. + Server capacity can be scaled independently of clients. When to use Almost any networked application with shared state: web, mobile backends, databases and email. Real-world applications A REST API serving web and mobile apps Database servers and JDBC clients SSH and SMTP. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Centralize state and logic behind a request protocol SCALABILITY Medium — replicate servers COUPLING Medium — protocol contract MAIN DRAWBACK Central server bottleneck / SPOF Disadvantages The server is a single point of failure and a bottleneck unless replicated. Clients depend on network availability. Chatty protocols create latency problems. Server evolution must stay compatible with old clients. When not to use Offline-first or fully decentralized scenarios (consider local-first or peer-to-peer). Key engineering considerations Version the API for old clients. Make servers stateless where possible. Budget for retries, timeouts and backpressure at the client. COMPLEXITY Low MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Any shared-state network app ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

I.05 Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Enterprise capabilities exposed as reusable, contractbased services, typically orchestrated through an Enterprise Service Bus (ESB). Compose business processes from shared services with standardized contracts (SOAP/WSDL, XML) mediated by middleware. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Siloed applications and point-to-point integrations in large enterprises. Introduced in the 2000s to reuse business capabilities across departments and integrate heterogeneous systems. Client Infrastructure Service / component External system Database / store Sync call How it works A channel calls an enterprise service through the ESB. The ESB looks up the service contract and routes the message. It transforms protocols and payload formats where needed. Composite processes are orchestrated centrally (BPEL-style). Services access shared enterprise data stores. Governance enforces schemas, versions and policies. SERVICE-ORIENTED ARCHITECTURE (SOA) Advantages Disadvantages Reuse of coarse-grained business capabilities. The ESB becomes a smart, monolithic bottleneck. + Integrates legacy and heterogeneous platforms. Heavy XML/SOAP contracts and tooling. Strong contracts and central governance. Shared databases couple services at the data layer. Central security and monitoring at the bus. Slow change cycles due to central governance. When to use When not to use Large enterprises integrating many legacy systems under strict governance and standard contracts. Fast-moving product teams that need independent deployment (prefer microservices); greenfield cloudnative systems. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Telecom billing and provisioning Insurance claims integration Bank core-system integration. Keep logic out of the bus where possible. Define canonical data models sparingly. Plan versioning and deprecation of service contracts. See SOA vs Microservices (Part IX). Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Enterprise-wide service reuse and integration COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium–High — via bus and shared data BEST USE CASE Legacy-heavy enterprise integration MAIN DRAWBACK ESB bottleneck and governance overhead ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

I.06 Microservices Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA An application built as independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its data, communicating over the network. Align service boundaries with business capabilities so small teams can build, deploy and scale each service autonomously. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Deployment coupling, team contention and uniform scaling in large monoliths. Popularized by Netflix, Amazon and others as cloud, containers and DevOps made independent services operable. Independent services behind a gateway, with sync and async communication Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works Clients call an API gateway, which routes to a service. A service executes within its own bounded context and data store. Synchronous calls are used for queries that need immediate answers. State changes are published as events for other services. Each service is built, deployed and scaled independently by its team. Service discovery, tracing and resilience patterns keep the mesh operable. MICROSERVICES ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Independent deployment and scaling per capability. + Fault isolation and technology freedom. Distributed-system complexity: latency, partial failure, eventual consistency. + Team autonomy aligned to the domain. Heavy operational load: CI/CD, observability, discovery, security. + Enables targeted resilience and ownership. Cross-service transactions need sagas. Poor boundaries create a distributed monolith. When to use When not to use Large systems with multiple teams, distinct scaling profiles, and high release frequency, where the organization has strong DevOps maturity. Small teams, unclear domain boundaries, low operational maturity, or when a modular monolith would suffice. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations E-commerce platforms Streaming services Payment and fintech platforms Draw boundaries by bounded context, not technical layer. Own one database per service. Standardize observability and idempotent retries. Start with fewer, coarser services and split with evidence. Ride-hailing backends. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Independent deployability and scaling of capabilities COMPLEXITY Very high SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium–High — if boundaries are right COUPLING Low — contract-based BEST USE CASE Large multi-team, high-scale systems MAIN DRAWBACK Operational and distributed-data complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

I.07 Modular Monolith Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A single deployable application whose internals are split into strongly encapsulated modules with explicit public APIs. Get microservice-style boundaries and team ownership without paying the network and operations cost. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED The big ball of mud in monoliths, and premature distribution. Teams that over-adopted microservices rediscovered that boundaries, not network hops, deliver most of the benefit. One deployable, modules communicate only via public interfaces Client Service / component Domain core Queue / broker Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Requests enter one application host. The host delegates to a module through its public API. Modules never access each other’s internals or tables. Cross-module reactions use in-process domain events. Each module owns its schema within the shared database. A module can later be extracted to a service along its existing boundary. I .07 MODULAR MONOLITH ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Strong boundaries with simple deployment and local transactions. Boundaries depend on discipline and tooling to stay enforced. Lower infra and operations cost than microservices. Single scaling and deployment unit remains. Refactoring across modules stays cheap. + Natural path to service extraction. A shared database can still tempt cross-module coupling. One bad module can affect process stability. When to use When not to use Mid-sized products, growing teams, and domains where service boundaries are still being discovered. Hard requirements for independent scaling, polyglot runtimes or fully independent release cadences. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Shopify’s large Rails monolith SaaS back offices Banking onboarding platforms. Enforce rules with Java modules, ArchUnit or Spring Modulith. Give each module its own schema and forbid cross-schema joins. Use domain events for crossmodule reactions. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Enforced boundaries inside one deployable SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Low — between modules MAIN DRAWBACK Single scale/release unit COMPLEXITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High BEST USE CASE Growing teams, uncertain boundaries ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

ANTI-PATTERN I.08 Distributed Monolith Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A system deployed as many services that are so tightly coupled they must be changed, released and scaled together. Not an intended design — it emerges when service boundaries ignore domain boundaries and coupling is kept. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Nothing; it is the failure mode that combines the cost of distribution with the coupling of a monolith. It appears when monoliths are split by technical layer or without ownership of data, or when services share a database. Client Service / component Database / store External system Sync call Dependency direction How it works A feature change spans services A, B and C. All three must be released together to stay compatible. Synchronous call chains make each request depend on all services. A shared database makes schema changes global. Failures cascade through the chain. Latency multiplies; independent scaling is impossible in practice. DISTRIBUTED MONOLITH ARCHITECTURE ANTI-PATTERN Advantages Disadvantages Teams may gain some code separation. + Can be a transitional state during migration. Network and operational cost with no autonomy gain. + Highlights where boundaries are wrong. Cascading failures and lock-step deployments. + Easier to fix than to live with — extracting data Hard to test and debug across services. ownership helps. Worse latency and availability than the original monolith. When to use When not to use Never as a goal. Recognize it as a transitional state while untangling a migration. Always. Merge tightly coupled services back, or redraw boundaries along bounded contexts with separate data. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Services split by layer (UI, logic, DB services) Microservices sharing one schema Release trains for “independent” services. Signals: simultaneous deploys, shared tables, deep synchronous chains, circular calls. Remedies: merge services, introduce events, give each service its data, introduce contract tests. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Not a goal — a diagnosis COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Low MAINTAINABILITY Low COUPLING Very high BEST USE CASE None MAIN DRAWBACK Pays for distribution without its benefits ARCHITECTURAL KIND Anti-pattern

DEPLOYMENT MODEL I.09 Serverless Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Applications built from managed services and shortlived functions where the provider handles servers, scaling and patching. Pay per invocation and compose managed building blocks (functions, queues, storage, auth) instead of running servers. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Idle capacity cost and the operational burden of capacity planning and patching. Cloud providers abstracted servers away (AWS Lambda, 2014) so teams could ship event-driven logic without infrastructure. Event-triggered functions composed with managed services Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works A client calls an API gateway or an event occurs (upload, message). The platform starts a function instance on demand. The function runs briefly and writes to managed storage. It emits an event or message to continue the workflow. The platform scales instances automatically, including to zero. Billing is per invocation and duration. SERVERLESS ARCHITECTURE DEPLOYMENT MODEL Advantages Disadvantages No server management; automatic elastic scaling. Cold starts and execution time limits. + Pay per use; cost-efficient for spiky workloads. Vendor lock-in and harder local testing. Fast to deliver event-driven features. Costly at sustained high throughput. Built-in high availability. Distributed debugging and state management are harder. When to use When not to use Spiky or low-traffic APIs, event processing, glue logic, data pipelines, and prototypes where operations staff is limited. Steady high-throughput workloads, long-running jobs, ultra-low-latency needs, or strict portability requirements. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Image/video processing on upload Webhook receivers Scheduled ETL jobs Design functions to be idempotent. Keep functions small and stateless. Watch concurrency limits, cold starts and per-call cost. See Serverless vs Containers (Part IX). Chatbot backends. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Run code without managing servers SCALABILITY Very high — auto-scaling COUPLING Low — via events MAIN DRAWBACK Cold starts, lock-in, limits COMPLEXITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Spiky/event-driven workloads ARCHITECTURAL Deployment model KIND

I.10 Event-Driven Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Components communicate by producing and reacting to events — immutable facts that something happened. Decouple producers from consumers through an event channel so each reacts independently and asynchronously. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Tight temporal and structural coupling of request/response calls between components. Systems needed real-time reactions, loose coupling and elastic scaling beyond what synchronous calls offered. Producers publish events to a broker; consumers react independently Service / component Queue / broker Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Something happens in a service (OrderPlaced). The service publishes an immutable event to a broker topic. The broker stores and delivers it to all interested consumers. Consumers process independently at their own pace. Consumers may emit new events, creating reaction chains. Failed processing is retried or routed to a dead-letter queue. EVENT-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Loose coupling; producers do not know consumers. + Easy to add new consumers without changing Eventual consistency and harder reasoning about flow. producers. Debugging and tracing event chains is difficult. Natural elasticity and buffering of spikes. + Enables real-time processing and audit trails. Requires idempotency, ordering and schema governance. Broker becomes critical infrastructure. When to use When not to use Workflows with many independent reactions, real-time analytics, integration between services, and spiky loads. Simple request/response needs, strictly synchronous results, or teams without messaging experience. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations E-commerce order lifecycle Fraud detection pipelines IoT telemetry Define event schemas with versioning (Avro/Protobuf + registry). Make consumers idempotent. Plan partitioning for ordering. Use outbox pattern for reliable publishing. See Event-Driven vs Message- Driven (Part IX). Notification systems. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Decoupled reaction to facts via events SCALABILITY Very high COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Eventual consistency and traceability COMPLEXITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Real-time, loosely coupled workflows ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

I.11 Peer-to-Peer Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A network of equal nodes that each act as both client and server, sharing resources directly without a central authority. Distribute load and responsibility across participants so capacity grows with the number of peers. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Central bottlenecks and single points of failure and control in client-server systems. Introduced for file sharing and later underpins blockchains and decentralized protocols. Peers connect directly; a tracker helps discovery only External system Client Sync call How it works A new peer contacts a bootstrap node or DHT to discover others. It connects to several peers and advertises what it holds. Requests are routed directly between peers. Data is replicated across peers for availability. Peers join and leave freely; the overlay self-heals. Integrity is verified by hashes or consensus rather than trusted servers. PEER-TO-PEER ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages No central point of failure; resilient to node loss. + Capacity scales with participants. Hard to guarantee consistency, security and quality of service. + Lower infrastructure cost for the provider. Discovery, NAT traversal and churn add complexity. + Censorship-resistant designs are possible. Difficult governance and updates. Malicious peers must be handled. When to use When not to use Content distribution, decentralized ledgers, collaboration with CRDTs, and resilient mesh or edge scenarios. Systems needing strong consistency, central authorization or predictable latency. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations BitTorrent Blockchain networks Plan peer discovery (DHT), NAT traversal, replication factor, trust model and rate limits. Choose consensus or CRDTs for shared state. WebRTC video calls IPFS. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Decentralized resource sharing among equals COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY High — grows with peers MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Decentralized distribution, ledgers MAIN DRAWBACK Weak consistency and security control ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

I.12 Distributed Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A system whose components run on multiple networked machines and coordinate by exchanging messages to appear as one system. Spread computation and data across nodes to gain scale, availability and locality, and accept partial failure as normal. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Limits of a single machine in capacity, throughput, availability and geographic reach. Data growth and availability demands exceeded vertical scaling; commodity clusters became the economical answer. Cluster with partitioned and replicated data, coordinated across nodes Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Requests are spread across nodes by a load balancer. Data is partitioned (sharded) so each node owns a subset. Each partition is replicated for availability. Nodes coordinate through consensus or a coordination service. Failures are detected via heartbeats and traffic is rerouted. The system trades consistency, latency and availability per CAP/PACELC choices. DISTRIBUTED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Horizontal scalability and high availability. + Geographic distribution reduces latency. Fault tolerance through replication. Cost-efficient on commodity hardware. When to use Systems exceeding a single node’s capacity or needing high availability and geographic reach. Real-world applications Search engines Distributed databases (Cassandra, Spanner) Large messaging platforms Global e-commerce. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Scale and availability via multiple nodes SCALABILITY Very high COUPLING Medium MAIN DRAWBACK Partial failure and consistency complexity Disadvantages Partial failures, network partitions and clock skew. Consistency is hard; debugging is hard. Operational and cognitive overhead. Cost of coordination and data movement. When not to use Workloads that comfortably fit on one reliable node; prefer a simpler design and replication for backup. Key engineering considerations Design for idempotency, retries with backoff, timeouts and circuit breakers. Choose consistency model explicitly. Plan partition tolerance, observability and chaos testing. COMPLEXITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Beyond single-node capacity ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

II.01 Clean Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Concentric layers — entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks — where source-code dependencies point only inward. Business rules must not depend on UI, database or frameworks; outer details plug into inner policy through interfaces. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Business logic entangled with frameworks and persistence, making change and testing expensive. Robert C. Martin consolidated Hexagonal, Onion and DCI ideas into one rule: the dependency rule. The dependency rule — all source dependencies point inward Client Database / store External system Service / component Domain core Module Sync call Dependency direction How it works A controller converts an HTTP request into a use-case input model. The use case orchestrates entities to apply business rules. It talks to persistence only through an output port (interface). An adapter in the outer layer implements that port against the database. The use case returns an output model; a presenter formats it for the view. Dependencies never point outward, so inner layers run without framework or DB. CLEAN ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Business logic is framework- and databaseindependent. More interfaces, mappers and boilerplate. Overkill for simple CRUD. + Highly testable: use cases run with in-memory fakes. Requires team discipline and shared understanding. + Replaceable UI, persistence and delivery Risk of ceremony without real domain complexity. mechanisms. + Strong separation supports long-lived systems. When to use When not to use Long-lived systems with non-trivial business rules, multiple delivery channels, or high testability needs. Throwaway prototypes, thin CRUD services, or very small teams with simple domains. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Core banking rules engines Insurance policy platforms Spring Boot services with rich domain logic. Place ports in the application layer and adapters in infrastructure. Keep entities free of framework annotations where practical. Test use cases without Spring. See Layered vs Clean vs Hexagonal vs Onion (Part IX). Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Make business rules independent of delivery and storage COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Very high COUPLING Low — inward only BEST USE CASE Complex, long-lived domains MAIN DRAWBACK Boilerplate and indirection ARCHITECTURAL KIND Code-organization approach

II.02 Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA An application core surrounded by ports (interfaces) with adapters that connect it to drivers (UI, tests) and driven systems (DB, messaging). Treat every external interaction — inbound or outbound — as an adapter plugged into a port owned by the core. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Business logic coupled to specific technologies and hard to test without infrastructure. Alistair Cockburn introduced it (2005) to make applications equally drivable by users, programs, tests and batch jobs. Core with inbound (driving) and outbound (driven) ports Client Module Domain core Service / component External system Database / store Queue / broker Sync call Dependency direction How it works A driving adapter (REST, listener, test) calls an inbound port. The domain service executes business logic inside the core. When it needs infrastructure, it calls an outbound port. A driven adapter implements that port (JPA, Kafka, HTTP client). Swapping adapters needs no change to the core. Tests drive the same inbound ports with fake driven adapters. HEXAGONAL ARCHITECTURE (PORTS AND ADAPTERS) Advantages Disadvantages Technology-agnostic core, easy to swap infrastructure. Extra interfaces and mapping layers. Port design requires judgment. + Uniform testing through ports. Can be overkill for trivial services. + Clear inbound/outbound boundaries. Team must hold the discipline. + Works well with DDD and event-driven edges. When to use When not to use Services with meaningful domain logic, many integrations, or the need to test without infrastructure and swap technologies. Simple pass-through APIs or short-lived scripts where ports add cost without value. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Payment orchestration services Integration-heavy order management Name ports by business intent, not technology. Keep adapters thin. Verify with architecture tests that core packages never import adapters. Microservices with Kafka and REST edges. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Isolate the core behind ports and adapters SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Low — core independent MAIN DRAWBACK Interface and mapping overhead COMPLEXITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Very high BEST USE CASE Integration-heavy domain services ARCHITECTURAL Code-organization approach KIND

II.03 Onion Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Layered rings around a domain model: domain model, domain services, application services, then infrastructure and UI on the outside. Make the domain model the center, with every outer ring depending inward, so infrastructure becomes a replaceable detail. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Traditional layering where the domain depends on the data layer. Jeffrey Palermo (2008) inverted the dependency between business and data access in layered designs. Concentric rings; dependencies point to the center Client Service / component External system Domain core Database / store Sync call Dependency direction How it works The UI calls an application service. The application service coordinates domain services and entities. Domain code expresses rules using the domain model only. Repository interfaces are defined in the domain ring. Infrastructure implements those interfaces and is wired at startup. Dependency injection keeps the center free of outer references. ONION ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Domain is independent of persistence and frameworks. More layers and indirection than classic layering. Requires dependency inversion discipline. + Strong testability of core logic. Mapping between rings adds boilerplate. + Clear separation of domain and application services. Ring boundaries can blur without enforcement. + Natural fit for DDD. When to use When not to use Domain-rich applications where infrastructure will change or the domain must be testable in isolation. Simple CRUD applications and prototypes. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations ERP domain modules Claims processing Pricing engines. Interfaces live inward, implementations outward. Wire with a DI container at the composition root. Treat the difference from Clean/Hexagonal as emphasis, not structure. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Put the domain model at the center COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Very high COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Domain-rich enterprise apps MAIN DRAWBACK Boilerplate and ring discipline ARCHITECTURAL KIND Code-organization approach

DESIGN APPROACH II.04 Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Structuring software around a model of the business domain using a ubiquitous language, bounded contexts and tactical building blocks. Strategic design splits the domain into bounded contexts; tactical design models rules with aggregates, entities, value objects and domain events. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED The gap between business understanding and code, and unclear service or module boundaries. Eric Evans (2003) addressed complex domains where technical models diverged from the business. Bounded contexts with a context map; aggregates inside each Domain core Module Queue / broker Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Domain experts and engineers build a ubiquitous language. The domain is split into bounded contexts with explicit boundaries. A context map defines relationships (customer–supplier, ACL, shared kernel). Inside a context, aggregates enforce invariants through one root. Domain events publish meaningful state changes to other contexts. An anti-corruption layer translates between models where needed. DOMAIN-DRIVEN DESIGN (DDD) ARCHITECTURE DESIGN APPROACH Advantages Disadvantages Code reflects business language and rules. High up-front modeling effort and learning curve. + Bounded contexts give natural microservice Overkill for CRUD domains. boundaries. Bad boundaries are expensive to fix. + Aggregates define transactional consistency clearly. Needs access to domain expertise. + Improves collaboration with domain experts. When to use When not to use Complex, evolving business domains such as finance, insurance and logistics, and as the basis for decomposing into services. Simple data-entry applications and domains without real behavior or invariants. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Payments and ledger systems Insurance policy management Logistics and fulfilment. Keep aggregates small and transactionally consistent; reference others by ID. Use events between contexts. Align team ownership to contexts. Pair with Hexagonal or Clean for code structure. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Model the business domain explicitly SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Low — between contexts MAIN DRAWBACK Modeling effort and expertise needed COMPLEXITY High MAINTAINABILITY Very high BEST USE CASE Complex business domains ARCHITECTURAL Design approach KIND

II.05 Screaming Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A structure where the top-level organization reveals the system’s purpose (billing, orders) rather than the framework (controllers, models). Package by business capability so the architecture “screams” what the system does. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Codebases whose folders say “Spring MVC” instead of what the product is for. Robert C. Martin argued that architecture should communicate intent, with frameworks as details. Package by capability, not by framework layer Module Sync call How it works Top-level folders are named after business capabilities. Each capability holds its own controllers, services and persistence. A new developer sees the domain at a glance. Frameworks live inside capabilities rather than defining structure. Cross-capability calls go through explicit public APIs. Capabilities can later become modules or services. SCREAMING ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Discoverability of purpose and features. Shared concerns need careful placement. + High cohesion within capabilities. Needs discipline to avoid cross-capability coupling. Easier ownership and modularization. + Frameworks stay replaceable details. Teams used to layer-based packaging need adjustment. Does not by itself define dependency rules. When to use When not to use Any codebase where discoverability by feature matters; a natural first step toward modules. Almost none; weak only where the domain is truly tiny. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spring Boot services packaged by feature Backend monorepos Package by feature, then apply Clean/Hexagonal rules inside each package. Use package-private visibility and architecture tests to keep boundaries. Modular monolith starters. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Make the code structure reveal intent COMPLEXITY Low SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low–Medium BEST USE CASE Discoverable feature-oriented code MAIN DRAWBACK No dependency rules by itself ARCHITECTURAL KIND Code-organization approach

II.06 Vertical Slice Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Code organized by feature (request → handler → data access), where each slice contains everything it needs end-to-end. Optimize for cohesion within a use case instead of abstraction across layers, so slices change independently. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Feature changes that touch every layer and shared abstractions that become over-general. Popularized by Jimmy Bogard as a reaction to heavy layering and generic service/repository abstractions. Each slice owns its full stack through a shared pipeline Client Infrastructure Service / component Module Database / store Sync call How it works A request maps to one use-case slice. A dispatcher runs shared behaviors (validation, auth, logging). The slice’s handler contains the logic for that feature only. The slice queries or updates the data store directly. Different slices may use different data access approaches. Adding a feature means adding a slice, not editing many layers. VERTICAL SLICE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Changes are localized to a feature. + Low coupling between features. Duplication across slices; needs refactoring discipline. + Each slice can choose the right technique (SQL, Fewer shared abstractions can hide domain concepts. ORM). + Fits CQRS-style command and query handlers. Inconsistent conventions without guidance. Less familiar to teams used to layers. When to use When not to use Feature-driven applications and APIs where teams ship by use case and domain logic is simple to moderate per feature. Domains with heavily shared complex rules unless a shared domain model is extracted. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Feature-oriented REST APIs .NET MediatR services Back-office applications. Extract shared domain logic only when duplication proves harmful. Use a mediator for cross-cutting behaviors. Keep slice tests at handler level. See Vertical Slice vs Layered (Part IX). Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Organize code by feature slices COMPLEXITY Low–Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low between slices BEST USE CASE Feature-driven APIs MAIN DRAWBACK Duplication and uneven conventions ARCHITECTURAL KIND Code-organization approach

II.07 Modular Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Decomposing software into cohesive modules with defined interfaces, hidden internals and explicit dependencies, independent of how they are deployed. Modularity is about boundaries and interfaces; deployment (one binary or many) is a separate decision. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Systems where any code can call any other code, causing ripple effects and no ownership. Information hiding (Parnas, 1972) remains the base principle behind libraries, plug-ins and services. Module Sync call Dependency direction How it works Identify cohesive capabilities and define module boundaries. Expose a small, stable public interface per module. Hide internals using visibility rules (JPMS, packages). Declare explicit module dependencies, avoiding cycles. Verify dependencies automatically in the build. Evolve modules independently within contract stability. I I .07 MODULAR ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Contained change and clear ownership. Poor boundaries are costly to correct. + Better testing and reuse. Interface design takes effort. Prerequisite for monoliths, plug-ins and services alike. Cycles and leaks creep in without enforcement. Versioning overhead for shared modules. + Enables parallel team work. When to use When not to use Any non-trivial codebase; essential for modular monoliths and before service extraction. Not applicable for production systems of any size; micro-modularizing tiny code is the failure mode. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Maven/Gradle multi-module builds Java Platform Module System (JPMS) Define API vs internal packages, enforce with ArchUnit/JPMS, keep dependency graphs acyclic, and version public contracts. OSGi bundles. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Encapsulation and explicit dependencies COMPLEXITY Low–Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Very high COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE All non-trivial codebases MAIN DRAWBACK Boundary design effort ARCHITECTURAL KIND Code-organization approach

II.08 Component-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A system composed of self-contained, replaceable components with well-defined provided and required interfaces. Build software by assembling reusable components that encapsulate behavior and communicate only through interfaces. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Monolithic code that cannot be reused, replaced or tested in parts. Component models (COM, EJB, OSGi) emerged to support reuse and assembly of larger systems. Components connected by provided and required interfaces Module Sync call How it works Decompose functionality into cohesive components. Each component declares provided and required interfaces. A container or composition root wires components together. Components interact only through interfaces. Components can be replaced or upgraded independently. Contracts are verified through interface tests. COMPONENT-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Reuse and replaceability. Interface and versioning overhead. + Parallel development against interfaces. Over-componentization adds indirection. Easier testing by mocking required interfaces. Runtime wiring can be complex. Lower coupling than monolithic code. Cross-component transactions are harder. When to use When not to use Large applications built from reusable pieces, UI frameworks and product lines with swappable parts. Small applications where a few classes suffice. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spring beans and DI React/Angular component trees OSGi plug-in bundles. Keep interfaces small and stable. Prefer composition over inheritance. Manage dependency direction and wiring through DI. UI-specific view: see Component- Based UI (Part IV). Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Assemble systems from replaceable components COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low–Medium — via interfaces BEST USE CASE Reusable, swappable parts MAIN DRAWBACK Interface and versioning overhead ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

II.09 Plugin-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A host application with a stable extension API into which third-party or optional plug-ins are loaded at runtime. Keep a small stable host and push variable features into independently developed plug-ins that conform to a contract. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Letting others extend an application without changing or recompiling its core. Ecosystems (IDEs, browsers, CMSs) need extensibility and isolation of optional features. Host application discovers and loads plug-ins through an extension API Domain core Module Infrastructure Service / component Sync call Dependency direction How it works The host exposes extension points and a plug-in contract. A registry discovers plug-ins (classpath, ServiceLoader, directory). Plug-ins are validated and loaded, optionally in isolated class loaders. The host calls plug-ins through the contract. Plug-ins may register UI, commands or handlers. Plug-ins are enabled, upgraded or removed without changing the core. PLUGIN-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Extensibility without core changes. API stability and versioning obligations. + Third-party ecosystem and optional features. Security and sandboxing concerns. Isolation of faulty extensions. Plug-in interactions are hard to test. Smaller core with faster stabilization. Dependency conflicts between plug-ins. When to use When not to use Platforms with an ecosystem: IDEs, build tools, CMSs, payment connectors, rule providers. Closed applications with no external extension need. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations IntelliJ and VS Code extensions Jenkins plugins Payment gateway connectors Freeze the contract and version it. Isolate class loaders, apply permissions and timeouts, and define a plug-in lifecycle. See Microkernel vs Plugin-Based (Part IX). Spring Boot starters. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Extend a stable host with optional plug-ins COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low — contract BEST USE CASE Ecosystems and optional features MAIN DRAWBACK API stability and security burden ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

II.10 Microkernel Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A minimal core system providing essential services, with additional functionality implemented as separate plug-in components or servers. Keep the kernel tiny and stable; everything else is replaceable and communicates through the kernel. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Large cores that are fragile to change and cannot support product variants. Born in operating systems (Mach, QNX) and later applied to product-line software. Small kernel with plug-in modules via a registry Client Domain core Service / component Sync call Async / event How it works Applications call the kernel API. The kernel provides minimal services: process management, messaging, registry. Feature modules register with the kernel. The kernel routes requests to the proper module. Modules run isolated from the core and each other. Product variants are built by choosing modules. MICROKERNEL ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Stable, small core; high reliability. Messaging overhead between kernel and modules. + Isolation: a failing module does not crash the kernel. Kernel API design is hard and hard to change. Flexible customization and portability. More moving parts than a monolith. Product-line friendly. Performance penalties on hot paths. When to use When not to use Operating systems, product-line applications, ruledriven systems with swappable features. Performance-critical single-purpose systems or apps without variability. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Operating-system microkernels Eclipse (core + plug-ins) Insurance rules per jurisdiction. Treat the kernel contract as sacrosanct. Separate core from optional features rigorously and measure intermodule overhead. Differences with plug-in designs are explained in Part IX. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Tiny core with replaceable modules SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Messaging overhead and core API rigidity COMPLEXITY High MAINTAINABILITY High BEST USE CASE OS and product-line systems ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

II.11 Micro-Frontends Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Splitting a web UI into independently developed and deployed frontend applications composed into one experience. Apply microservice thinking to the frontend: vertical teams own a feature from UI to API. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Monolithic frontends where many teams block each other on one codebase and release. Large web apps outgrew single SPA teams; module federation and edge composition made runtime composition practical. A shell composes independently deployed frontends, each with its backend Client Infrastructure Service / component Sync call Async / event How it works The browser loads a shell from a CDN. The shell resolves which micro-frontends to mount for the route. Each micro-frontend bundle is fetched from its own deployment. Composition happens via module federation, web components, iframes or edge includes. Each team calls its own backend. Cross-MFE communication uses events or shared contracts, not shared state. MICRO-FRONTENDS ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Independent team autonomy and deployment. Duplication of dependencies and bundle weight. + Incremental upgrades and technology freedom. Inconsistent UX without a design system. Scales organizations, not just code. Integration and versioning complexity. Fault isolation by feature. More build and runtime infrastructure. When to use When not to use Large products with many teams that own distinct sections of a web experience. Small teams or apps where a single well-structured SPA is sufficient. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Large e-commerce sites Enterprise portals Banking digital channels. Share a design system and minimal runtime contract. Avoid shared global state. Measure bundle size and use performance budgets. See also Part IV (UI architectures). Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Independent deployment of UI features COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Many teams, large web products MAIN DRAWBACK UX consistency and bundle overhead ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

II.12 Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A dedicated backend per client experience (web, mobile, partner) that aggregates and shapes downstream service data. Give each frontend its own tailor-made API layer so general-purpose services do not accumulate clientspecific logic. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED One-size-fits-all APIs that cause over-fetching, chatty calls and conflicting client requirements. Mobile and web clients diverged in needs; Sam Newman and SoundCloud popularized per-client backends. One BFF per client type in front of shared domain services Client Service / component Sync call How it works A client calls its own BFF. The BFF authenticates, then fans out to the domain services it needs. It aggregates, filters and reshapes responses for that client. It handles client-specific concerns: pagination, payload size, protocol. Domain services stay generic and stable. Each BFF is owned and released by the client team. BACKEND-FOR-FRONTEND (BFF) ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Optimized payloads and fewer round trips per client. + Client teams move independently. More services to run and duplicate logic across BFFs. + Keeps client logic out of core services. Risk of logic drift between BFFs. + Different protocols (GraphQL, REST) per client. Another hop adds latency. Needs clear ownership. When to use When not to use Multiple client types with different data and interaction needs on a shared service backend. A single client, or when a gateway with simple routing is sufficient. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spotify and SoundCloud client backends Retail web vs mobile apps Keep BFFs thin and free of domain rules. Share libraries for cross-BFF concerns. Add caching and timeouts per downstream. See API Gateway (Part V). Mobile banking. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Client-specific backend aggregation COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low–Medium BEST USE CASE Several client types on shared services MAIN DRAWBACK Duplicate logic and extra hop ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern
