III.01 Pipe-and-Filter Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A chain of independent processing steps (filters) connected by channels (pipes), each transforming its input stream into an output stream. Build complex processing from small, single-purpose filters that share only a data format. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Monolithic processing code that is hard to reuse, reorder, test or parallelize. Unix pipelines and compilers showed that composable transformations scale from shell scripts to ETL and media processing. Data flows through filters connected by pipes External system Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works A source emits raw data into the first pipe. Each filter reads input, applies one transformation and writes output. Pipes buffer data and decouple filter speeds. Filters are stateless and know nothing about neighbors. The sink persists or exposes the final result. Filters can be reordered, replaced or run in parallel. PIPE-AND-FILTER ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages High reuse and composability of filters. Poor fit for interactive or stateful workflows. + Easy to test each step in isolation. Data format conversions between filters add + Natural parallelism and streaming. overhead. + Simple mental model. Error handling across the chain is awkward. Sharing global state is difficult. When to use When not to use Data transformation, ETL, compilers, media and log processing, and request-processing chains. Interactive applications, workflows with complex branching and shared state. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Unix shell pipelines Log enrichment pipelines Standardize the data contract between filters. Add backpressure and a dead-letter path for bad records. Keep filters idempotent and stateless where possible. Spring Integration flows Image processing chains. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Compose transformations as a chain of filters COMPLEXITY Low SCALABILITY High — parallel filters MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Streaming and ETL transformations MAIN DRAWBACK Poor for stateful interactive workflows ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

III.02 Publish–Subscribe Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Publishers send messages to topics without knowing subscribers; subscribers receive messages for topics they have subscribed to. A broker mediates delivery so producers and consumers are decoupled in time, space and quantity. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Point-to-point integration where each producer must know and call every consumer. Real-time feeds and large integration landscapes needed one-to-many distribution without coupling. A topic fans out one message to many subscribers Service / component Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works A publisher sends a message to a named topic. The broker stores or routes it to all current subscriptions. Each subscriber receives its own copy. Subscribers acknowledge; the broker tracks delivery per subscription. New subscribers can join without touching the publisher. Failures are retried or sent to a dead-letter topic. PUBLISH–SUBSCRIBE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Loose coupling and easy fan-out. Delivery guarantees and ordering are non-trivial. + Add or remove consumers without publisher Hard to know who consumed what. changes. Duplicates require idempotent consumers. + Scalable one-to-many distribution. The broker is critical infrastructure. + Buffers load spikes. When to use When not to use Notifications, cache invalidation, real-time feeds, and broadcasting domain events. Request/response exchanges needing an immediate reply, or strict transactional workflows. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Price and inventory updates Push notifications Choose delivery semantics per topic (at-least-once with idempotence). Use consumer groups to scale. Monitor lag and set retention policies. Cache invalidation Stock market feeds. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE One-to-many decoupled message distribution COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Fan-out of events and updates MAIN DRAWBACK Delivery and ordering semantics ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

III.03 Message-Driven Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Components communicate through asynchronous messages, often targeted commands or requests, delivered via queues with a specific recipient. Messages are addressed work or data items; the sender expects some component to handle them, decoupling timing and failure. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Blocking calls and availability coupling between components. Enterprise messaging (JMS, AMQP) enabled reliable asynchronous work distribution. Producer sends commands to a queue; competing consumers process them Service / component Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works A sender creates a message addressed to a queue or endpoint. The broker persists it until a consumer is available. One consumer from a pool receives and processes it. The consumer acknowledges success; failures are redelivered. Poison messages move to a dead-letter queue. Results may flow back through a reply queue or a follow-up message. MESSAGE-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Temporal decoupling and reliable delivery. Asynchronous complexity and eventual results. + Load leveling and easy horizontal scaling of Requires idempotency and ordering strategy. workers. Debugging message flows is harder. + Failure isolation and retries. Broker operations and capacity planning. + Back-pressure through queue depth. When to use When not to use Background processing, work distribution, command handling, integrations needing guaranteed delivery. Interactions that need immediate synchronous responses. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Payment processing workers Email sending Make consumers idempotent. Set visibility timeouts, retry policies and DLQs. Size worker pools from queue depth. See Event-Driven vs Message-Driven (Part IX). Order fulfillment commands Batch job dispatch. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Asynchronous addressed messages via queues COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low–Medium BEST USE CASE Reliable background work MAIN DRAWBACK Async complexity and ops overhead ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

COMMUNICATION PATTERN III.04 Request–Response Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A requester sends a message and waits for a correlated response from the receiver. The simplest interaction model: a synchronous exchange where the caller needs the result to continue. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Giving callers immediate results with straightforward semantics and error handling. It maps naturally to function calls and underlies HTTP, RPC and database access. Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store External system Sync call How it works The client sends a request and starts a timeout. The service validates and authorizes it. It performs work, possibly calling dependencies synchronously. It returns a response with data or an error status. The client handles success, error or timeout. Retries must be idempotent and use backoff. REQUEST–RESPONSE ARCHITECTURE COMMUNICATION PATTERN Advantages Disadvantages Simple semantics and debugging. Temporal coupling: callee must be up. + Immediate feedback and strong consistency Cascading failures and latency amplification. possible. Harder to scale spiky loads without buffering. + Wide tooling and protocol support. Chains of calls accumulate latency. + Easy to secure and observe. When to use When not to use Queries, user-facing operations, short transactions and anything the caller needs to know immediately. Long-running tasks, fan-out notifications or workloads that must survive downstream outages. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations REST/gRPC APIs Database queries Authentication checks. Always set timeouts, retries with jitter and circuit breakers. Propagate deadlines. Make mutating retries idempotent. See Synchronous vs Asynchronous (Part IX). Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Synchronous correlated exchange COMPLEXITY Low SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING High — temporal BEST USE CASE Queries and immediate results MAIN DRAWBACK Cascading failures and latency ARCHITECTURAL KIND Communication pattern

III.05 Event Sourcing WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Persist state as an append-only sequence of immutable events; current state is derived by replaying them. The event log is the source of truth; state is a projection of history. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Lost history, hard audit trails and difficulty reconstructing how state came to be. Domains like finance and ledgers need complete audit and temporal queries; also enables replay and new projections. Commands append events; state and views are derived by replay Client Domain core Database / store Infrastructure Queue / broker Service / component Sync call Async / event How it works A command is validated against the aggregate’s current state. The aggregate emits one or more events. Events are appended to the event store atomically. Current state is rebuilt by replaying events, accelerated by snapshots. Events are published to projectors and other services. New views are created by replaying history. EVENT SOURCING Advantages Disadvantages Complete audit log and time-travel queries. + Easily build new read models retroactively. Steeper learning curve; eventual consistency of views. + Natural integration events and debugging by replay. Event schema evolution is difficult. + Append-only writes are fast. Querying current state requires projections. Replay and storage cost grows over time. When to use When not to use Ledgers, financial and compliance domains, collaborative systems, and domains needing history or undo. Simple CRUD, or teams unprepared for versioning and projection complexity. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Banking ledgers Order lifecycle tracking Audit-heavy systems Version events from day one (upcasters). Use snapshots for long streams. Make projectors idempotent. Plan GDPR deletion strategies (cryptoshredding). See CQRS vs Event Sourcing (Part IX). Collaborative editing. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE State as an immutable event log COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Audit-heavy transactional domains MAIN DRAWBACK Schema evolution and complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

III.06 CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Separate models for writing state (commands) and reading it (queries), often with distinct stores. Writes and reads have different needs, so optimize each side independently. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED A single model that is poorly suited to both complex business rules and rich, high-volume queries. Read-heavy systems with complex query needs outgrew a single normalized model. Separate write and read paths, synchronized by events Client Service / component Database / store Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works Commands go to a handler that applies business rules to the write model. The write store is updated transactionally. Changes are published as events or via change data capture. A projector updates the denormalized read store. Queries read only from the read model. Read and write sides scale independently. CQRS (COMMAND QUERY RESPONSIBILITY SEGREGATION) Advantages Disadvantages Independent optimization and scaling of reads and writes. Eventual consistency between sides. More components and synchronization logic. + Simpler, purpose-built models. Over-engineering for simple domains. + Fast queries from denormalized views. Duplicated data and operational cost. + Fits event-driven systems. When to use When not to use Read-heavy systems, complex domain writes with varied read views, and reporting alongside transactions. Straightforward CRUD, or when users cannot tolerate stale reads and a single model works. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Product catalog with search Order history views Banking balance and statement views. Handle read-your-own-writes explicitly. Make projections idempotent and rebuildable. Monitor replication lag. Do not confuse with Event Sourcing — they combine but are independent. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Separate write and read models COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Read-heavy, complex domains MAIN DRAWBACK Eventual consistency and extra moving parts ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

III.07 CQRS with Event Sourcing WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA The write side stores events as the source of truth (Event Sourcing) and the read side builds query models from those events (CQRS). Combine an immutable event log for writes with projections for reads to get audit, replay and tailored query models. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Needs for full history plus fast, flexible queries in complex domains. The two patterns complement each other: events are the natural synchronization mechanism between write and read models. Event store feeds multiple projections; commands and queries are separate Client Service / component Database / store Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works A command loads an aggregate by replaying its events. Business rules run and new events are appended with optimistic concurrency. Events are published to the bus. Projectors build one or more read models. Queries are served from the read stores. Rebuilding a read model means replaying the event stream. I I I .07 CQRS WITH EVENT SOURCING Advantages Disadvantages Full audit trail plus optimized reads. Highest conceptual and operational complexity. + Add new views without migrating the write side. Eventual consistency everywhere. Temporal queries and debugging by replay. Event versioning and replay cost. Fits event-driven integration. Specialized skills required. When to use When not to use Complex regulated domains such as banking ledgers, trading, and insurance, where audit and multiple read views are first-class requirements. Most business systems. Use plain CQRS or CRUD unless history and replay are real requirements. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Trading and settlement systems Core banking ledgers Invest in tooling: event schema registry, replay tooling, projection monitoring. Keep aggregates small. Plan snapshotting and archival. Booking engines with audit. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Event-sourced writes with projected reads COMPLEXITY Very high SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Audit-heavy, multi-view domains MAIN DRAWBACK Complexity and skill requirement ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

III.08 Saga Pattern WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A long-running business transaction split into local transactions across services, with compensating actions to undo completed steps on failure. Replace distributed ACID transactions with a sequence of local commits and explicit compensations. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Maintaining consistency across services that own separate databases without two-phase commit. Microservices with database-per-service cannot use a single transaction; sagas (Garcia-Molina, 1987) provide eventual consistency. Booking saga with compensations (orchestrated) Client Service / component Sync call Async / event How it works The saga starts and the first local transaction commits. Each step triggers the next via command or event. If a step fails, the saga stops moving forward. Compensating transactions undo earlier steps in reverse order. Saga state is persisted so it can recover from crashes. All steps and compensations must be idempotent. SAGA PAT T E R N Advantages Disadvantages Consistency without distributed locks or 2PC. + Services stay autonomous and available. Only eventual consistency; no isolation between steps. + Works with heterogeneous data stores. Compensation logic is complex to design. + Explicit business-level failure handling. Hard to reason about and test failure paths. Intermediate states are visible to others. When to use When not to use Multi-service business processes such as orders, bookings and payments where each service owns its data. Operations needing strict atomicity and isolation; if two things always change together, keep them in one service. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations E-commerce checkout Travel booking (flight + hotel + car) Money transfer between ledgers. Choose orchestration or choreography per saga. Use semantic locks to limit anomalies. Persist state, use timeouts and make every step idempotent. See Orchestration vs Choreography (Part IX). Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Distributed consistency via compensations COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Cross-service business transactions MAIN DRAWBACK No isolation; compensation complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

III.09 Choreography-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Services coordinate a process by reacting to each other’s events, with no central controller. Each service knows what to do when it sees certain events, and emits events of its own. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Central coordinators becoming bottlenecks and coupling points in event-driven systems. Event-driven microservices naturally lend themselves to decentralized coordination. Service / component Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works The Order service publishes OrderCreated. Payment reacts, charges and publishes PaymentCompleted. Inventory reacts, reserves stock and publishes StockReserved. Shipping reacts and starts fulfillment. On failures services publish compensating events. No component owns the full process view. CHOREOGRAPHY-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Loose coupling and no central bottleneck. Process logic is spread across services. + Easy to add new participants by subscribing. Hard to see, test and debug end-to-end. Services remain autonomous. Risk of cyclic dependencies between events. Simple for short flows. Compensation and timeouts are hard to track. When to use When not to use Simple, short event chains with few participants and high autonomy needs. Complex flows with many steps, branching or strict visibility requirements — prefer orchestration. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Order → payment → inventory pipelines Notification fan-out Document the event flow, add correlation IDs, and trace with distributed tracing. Watch for hidden coupling via event content. User sign-up side effects. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Decentralized event-reaction workflows COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Low–Medium — flow hard to trace COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Simple, autonomous chains MAIN DRAWBACK Flow visibility and debugging ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

III.10 Orchestration-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A central orchestrator controls a business process by calling participating services in a defined order and handling failures. Centralize workflow logic in one component that commands services and tracks state. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Opaque, scattered process logic in choreographed systems. Complex workflows need visibility, timeouts and compensation in one place; engines like Camunda and Temporal address this. Orchestrator sends commands and tracks workflow state Client Service / component Database / store Sync call How it works The orchestrator starts a workflow instance. It sends a command to the first service and waits for the result. It persists state after each step to survive crashes. It chooses the next step or compensation based on results. Timeouts and retries are managed centrally. The full process is visible and inspectable in one place. ORCHESTRATION-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages End-to-end visibility and control. + Easier to implement complex logic and Orchestrator can become a bottleneck or a god service. compensation. Added coupling to the orchestrator. Central monitoring and timeout handling. Requires high availability of the workflow engine. + Simplifies participating services. Risk of putting business logic in the wrong place. When to use When not to use Multi-step processes with branching, human steps, SLAs and compensation requirements. Simple two-step interactions, or when services must stay entirely decoupled. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Loan origination Order fulfillment Keep the orchestrator free of domain rules — it coordinates, services decide. Use durable-execution engines. Version workflow definitions. Payment settlement workflows Onboarding. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Central control of multi-service workflows COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium–High COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Complex, visible workflows MAIN DRAWBACK Orchestrator as a coupling point ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

III.11 Space-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Processing units with in-memory data grids replicated across a virtualized middleware, removing the central database as a bottleneck. Keep hot data in a distributed in-memory grid next to the processing and write back to the database asynchronously. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Database bottlenecks and scalability limits under extreme and unpredictable load. Derived from tuple-space ideas (JavaSpaces, GigaSpaces) for high-volume transactional systems. Processing units with replicated in-memory grid; asynchronous persistence Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works A request hits any processing unit via the load balancer. The PU reads and writes data in its in-memory grid replica. The data grid replicates changes to other PUs. A data writer persists changes to the database asynchronously. The deployment manager spins up more PUs under load. On failure, another PU holds the replicated data. SPACE-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Extreme elasticity and low latency. Complex to build and operate. + Removes database as the scaling bottleneck. Data consistency and synchronization overhead. High availability through replicated memory. Memory cost and limited dataset size. Suitable for unpredictable spikes. Hard to test and to model analytics. When to use When not to use Highly variable, high-volume systems such as online auctions, ticketing and trading front ends. Large data sets that do not fit in memory, or typical transactional business apps. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Online ticket sales Auction platforms Define data ownership and partitioning rules. Tune write-behind durability and reconciliation. Test failover and cache warm-up. Real-time bidding Gaming session state. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE In-memory grid to remove DB bottleneck COMPLEXITY Very high SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Low–Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Spiky, high-throughput transactional load MAIN DRAWBACK Complexity and memory-bound data ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

III.12 Shared-Nothing Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Each node is self-sufficient — owns its own CPU, memory and disk — and nodes share no state; they coordinate only over the network. Partition data and work so no node contends for shared resources, giving near-linear scale-out. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Contention and single points of failure caused by shared disks, memory or locks. Stonebraker (1986) proposed it for parallel databases; it underpins modern scale-out data systems. Independent nodes each own a data partition Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Data is partitioned by a key across nodes. A router sends each request to the node owning the data. Each node reads and writes only its local storage. Nodes replicate partitions to peers for fault tolerance. Adding nodes adds capacity; data is rebalanced. Cross-partition queries are coordinated at the router or client. SHARED-NOTHING ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Near-linear horizontal scalability. Cross-partition joins and transactions are hard. + No shared bottlenecks or single point of contention. Partitioning keys must be chosen well (hot spots). Failure of a node affects only its partition (with replicas). Rebalancing is operationally complex. Application must be partition-aware. + Commodity hardware. When to use When not to use Massive-scale databases and services with partitionable workloads and key-based access. Workloads dominated by cross-entity transactions or ad-hoc joins. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Cassandra and DynamoDB Sharded MySQL Choose partition keys by access pattern. Plan resharding and replication factor. Denormalize to avoid cross-partition joins. Elasticsearch clusters. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Independent nodes with no shared state COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Partitionable, key-based workloads MAIN DRAWBACK Cross-partition queries and transactions ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

III.13 Blackboard Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Independent specialist components (knowledge sources) cooperate by reading and writing a shared data structure (the blackboard), coordinated by a controller. When no deterministic algorithm exists, let specialists incrementally refine partial solutions on a shared space. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Problems with uncertain, incremental solutions such as speech recognition or signal interpretation. Originated in the Hearsay-II speech recognition system (1970s) for non-deterministic problem solving. Knowledge sources contribute to a shared blackboard under a controller Service / component Database / store Domain core Sync call How it works Initial data is placed on the blackboard. The controller watches the blackboard for changes. It selects and activates the knowledge source best suited to progress. The knowledge source reads partial results and posts new hypotheses. Iteration continues until a satisfactory solution emerges. The controller decides termination. BLACKBOARD ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Handles ill-defined problems with no fixed algorithm. Difficult to test and reason about; non-deterministic. Shared state creates coupling to the data model. + Modular, replaceable knowledge sources. Controller design is complex. + Supports incremental refinement and experimentation. Performance and concurrency control are hard. + Easy to add expertise. When to use When not to use AI, speech and image recognition, sensor fusion and diagnostics systems. Well-defined business transactions with deterministic logic. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Speech recognition research systems Sensor-fusion and threat analysis Medical diagnostic assistants. Define the blackboard data model carefully. Control concurrency with locks or versioned entries. Instrument which knowledge source made each change. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Opportunistic collaboration on shared state SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium MAIN DRAWBACK Hard to test and control COMPLEXITY High MAINTAINABILITY Low–Medium BEST USE CASE Non-deterministic problem solving ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

III.14 Broker Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A broker component mediates between clients and servers, handling discovery, routing and communication so they remain decoupled. Clients address services logically; the broker locates and invokes them, hiding location and protocol. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Direct dependencies and hard-coded endpoints between distributed components. CORBA-era distributed objects and modern message brokers need a mediator to manage heterogeneity and location. Client Infrastructure Service / component Sync call How it works Servers register their services with the broker. A client sends a request addressed logically to the broker. The broker locates a suitable server. It marshals the request and forwards it. The server processes it and returns a result via the broker. The broker returns the result to the client. BROKER ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Location transparency and loose coupling. Broker is a bottleneck and single point of failure. + Central routing, security and monitoring. Extra hop adds latency. Servers can change without client impact. Operational complexity. Supports heterogeneous platforms. Can accumulate logic (smart pipes). When to use When not to use Systems integrating heterogeneous components, message-oriented middleware and service discovery scenarios. Simple point-to-point systems; latency-critical paths. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations RabbitMQ / ActiveMQ based integration CORBA ORBs Cluster the broker, keep it dumb, and monitor throughput and queue depth. Define clear contracts and versioning. API management layers. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Mediated location-transparent communication COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium–High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Heterogeneous integration MAIN DRAWBACK Bottleneck and SPOF ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

III.15 Batch Processing Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Process large volumes of data in scheduled, bounded jobs rather than continuously. Collect data over a window, then process it as a whole for throughput and efficiency. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Heavy computation over large datasets where latency is not critical. The original mainframe processing model; still the most cost-effective for large-scale transformations and reporting. Scheduled jobs read, process and write in chunks Infrastructure Database / store Service / component Sync call How it works A scheduler triggers the job at a set time. The job reads input in chunks. Each chunk is processed and validated. Results are written with commit checkpoints. Failures restart from the last checkpoint. The job reports status and metrics on completion. BATCH PROCESSING ARCHITECTURE Advantages High throughput and efficient resource use. + Simple, deterministic and re-runnable. Cheap compute (off-peak). Easy to audit and test with fixed inputs. When to use Nightly settlements, billing, reporting, ETL and data migration. Real-world applications End-of-day bank settlements Payroll runs Data warehouse loads Spring Batch jobs. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Scheduled bulk processing SCALABILITY High COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK High latency / stale data Disadvantages High latency; data is stale between runs. Failures late in a run are expensive. Peaks in resource usage and batch windows. Not suitable for real-time needs. When not to use Real-time or interactive needs; use stream processing instead. Key engineering considerations Make jobs idempotent and restartable. Use chunking and checkpoints. Monitor SLAs for batch windows. See Lambda vs Kappa (Part IX). COMPLEXITY Low–Medium MAINTAINABILITY High BEST USE CASE Large offline workloads ARCHITECTURAL Architectural style KIND

III.16 Stream Processing Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Continuous processing of unbounded event streams in near real time, with stateful operators and windowing. Treat data as an infinite stream and compute incrementally as events arrive. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED The latency of batch for use cases needing immediate insight or reaction. Real-time analytics, fraud detection and monitoring required sub-second processing at scale. Kafka topics processed by a stateful stream processor External system Queue / broker Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Producers publish events to a log such as Kafka. A stream processor consumes events continuously. It applies filters, joins and windowed aggregations. Operator state is kept in local stores with checkpoints. Results are emitted to topics, stores or alerts. On failure the job restarts from the last checkpoint with exactly-once or at-least-once semantics. STREAM PROCESSING ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Low-latency insight and reaction. + Continuous, incremental computation. Stateful processing and exactly-once semantics are hard. + Scales with partitions. Late and out-of-order events require watermarking. + Replayable from the log. Operational complexity of stream clusters. Harder debugging than batch. When to use When not to use Fraud detection, monitoring, real-time personalization and IoT analytics. Workloads fine with periodic batch; small data where simple queries suffice. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Payment fraud scoring Clickstream analytics Define event-time semantics and windows. Size state and checkpoint intervals. Handle reprocessing via replay. Partition keys determine parallelism. Ride surge pricing IoT alerting. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Continuous real-time computation on streams COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Real-time analytics and reactions MAIN DRAWBACK State, ordering and late-data complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

III.17 Lambda Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Combines a batch layer for accurate historical views with a speed layer for real-time views, merged by a serving layer. Use batch for correctness and stream for freshness, then query both together. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Getting low-latency results while still computing complete and corrected results. Nathan Marz proposed it when stream systems were less reliable than batch for accuracy. Batch and speed layers merged in a serving layer External system Queue / broker Service / component Database / store Client Sync call Async / event How it works All data is appended to an immutable master dataset. The batch layer recomputes accurate views periodically. The speed layer computes incremental views for recent data. The serving layer merges batch and real-time views. Batch results eventually supersede speed-layer approximations. Queries see a unified, fresh view. LAMBDA ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Accurate results plus low latency. Two code paths for the same logic. + Fault tolerance through recomputation. Operational overhead of both systems. Clear separation of concerns. Divergence between layers causes inconsistencies. Works with mixed technologies. Often superseded by Kappa or lakehouse streaming. When to use When not to use Systems needing both historical accuracy and realtime views when streaming alone cannot give correct results. When one reliable streaming engine can serve both; prefer Kappa. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Legacy analytics platforms Ad-tech reporting Share business logic between layers where possible. Test layer equivalence. Define reconciliation rules for the merge. See Lambda vs Kappa (Part IX). Metrics systems combining daily and live data. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Batch accuracy plus speed-layer freshness COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Low–Medium — dual logic COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Accurate + real-time analytics MAIN DRAWBACK Duplicate logic across two layers ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

III.18 Kappa Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A single stream-processing pipeline over a replayable log handles both real-time and reprocessing. Use one codebase and treat batch as replaying the log through the same stream job. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Lambda’s duplicated logic and operational complexity. Jay Kreps proposed it as stream engines matured and logs such as Kafka became durable and replayable. One streaming path; reprocessing by replaying the log External system Queue / broker Service / component Database / store Client Sync call Async / event How it works All data is written to a durable, replayable log. A stream job processes events and writes to a serving store. Logic changes are deployed as a new job version. The new job replays the log from the start into a new output table. When caught up, traffic switches to the new output. The old job and table are retired. KAPPA ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Single codebase and processing model. Needs long retention and strong stream engine. + Simpler operations than Lambda. Reprocessing large history can be slow and costly. Easy reprocessing via replay. Complex stateful jobs remain hard. Consistent results for batch and real time. Less suitable for heavy ad-hoc batch analytics. When to use When not to use Event-centric systems with replayable logs where a unified stream pipeline can satisfy accuracy needs. Workloads needing complex historical batch computation that streaming engines handle poorly. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Real-time analytics on Kafka Size log retention and storage tiers. Version jobs and outputs. Test replay performance before relying on it. Fraud pipelines Event-sourced systems reprocessing. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Stream-only processing with replay for reprocessing COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium–High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Unified event analytics MAIN DRAWBACK Replay cost and engine maturity needs ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

IV.01 MVC (Model-View-Controller) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Separates an application into Model (data and rules), View (presentation) and Controller (input handling that updates the model and selects the view). Keep presentation, input handling and business data apart so each can change independently. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED UI code that mixes rendering, input handling and business logic into unmaintainable screens. Introduced in Smalltalk-80 and became the standard for server-rendered web frameworks (Spring MVC, Rails, ASP.NET MVC). Controller mediates; the view observes or reads the model Client Service / component Domain core Database / store Sync call How it works The user triggers an action (HTTP request or UI event). The controller interprets the input and validates it. The controller calls the model to perform the operation. The model updates state or reads data from storage. The controller selects a view and passes it model data. The view renders the response to the user. MVC (MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER) Advantages Disadvantages Clear separation of concerns. Controllers can become “fat” and tangled. + Parallel work on UI and business logic. View–model coupling varies by implementation. Multiple views for the same model. Hard to unit test views. Mature framework support. Rich client state is awkward in the classic form. When to use When not to use Server-rendered web applications and APIs with request-driven interaction. Highly interactive, stateful client UIs where two-way binding or unidirectional state fits better. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spring MVC web apps Ruby on Rails Keep controllers thin: delegate to services. Do not put domain logic in views. See MVC vs MVP vs MVVM vs MVI (Part IX). ASP.NET MVC. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Separate model, view and input handling COMPLEXITY Low SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Server-rendered web apps MAIN DRAWBACK Fat controllers ARCHITECTURAL KIND UI pattern

IV.02 MVP (Model-View-Presenter) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA The Presenter holds all presentation logic and updates a passive View through an interface; the View forwards events to the Presenter. Make the view as dumb as possible so presentation logic can be unit tested without the UI framework. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Untestable UI logic embedded in views and the tight coupling of MVC views to models. Evolved from MVC for desktop and Android UIs where views were hard to test. Passive view; presenter updates it via an interface Client Service / component Domain core Sync call How it works The user interacts with the view. The view forwards the event to the presenter. The presenter calls the model to process the action. The model returns data or results. The presenter formats the data for presentation. The presenter calls methods on the view interface to render it. MVP (MODEL-VIEW-PRESENTER) Advantages Disadvantages Highly testable presenters using mocked views. Boilerplate view interfaces and glue code. + Clear one-to-one presenter/view relationship. Presenters can grow large. View is simple and replaceable. Manual synchronization of state to the view. No binding framework required. Lifecycle handling adds complexity. When to use When not to use UIs needing strong testability without data binding frameworks, such as classic Android or desktop apps. Frameworks with declarative binding where MVVM reduces glue code. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Android apps (pre-Jetpack) WinForms applications Define a minimal IView contract. Keep presenters free of framework classes. Handle lifecycle by attaching and detaching the view. GWT apps. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Passive view with presenter logic SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium — presenter↔view MAIN DRAWBACK Boilerplate and manual sync COMPLEXITY Low–Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium–High BEST USE CASE Testable classic UIs ARCHITECTURAL UI pattern KIND

IV.03 MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA The ViewModel exposes observable state and commands; the View binds to them declaratively and the ViewModel knows nothing about the view. Use data binding so the view updates automatically when ViewModel state changes. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Glue code in MVP and tight coupling between views and presentation logic. Introduced by Microsoft for WPF/Silverlight and adopted by Android Jetpack, Vue and Angular. Two-way binding between view and view-model Client Service / component Domain core Database / store Sync call How it works The user interacts with a bound control. Binding invokes a command or updates a property in the ViewModel. The ViewModel calls the model or repositories. The model returns data asynchronously. The ViewModel updates observable state. The binding engine re-renders the view automatically. MVVM (MODEL-VIEW-VIEWMODEL) Advantages Disadvantages Minimal glue code through binding. Binding can be hard to debug. + ViewModel is testable without UI. ViewModels can bloat; overhead for simple screens. Views stay declarative and swappable. Memory leaks with improper subscriptions. Works well with reactive streams. Two-way binding hides data flow. When to use When not to use Rich client UIs with a binding framework: Android Jetpack, WPF, Angular, Vue. Very simple screens or platforms without binding support. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Android apps with ViewModel + LiveData/Flow WPF enterprise tools Expose immutable state from ViewModels. Avoid view references in the ViewModel. Handle one-time events explicitly. Vue applications. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Declarative binding of view to state SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Low — binding only MAIN DRAWBACK Binding opacity and ViewModel bloat COMPLEXITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High BEST USE CASE Rich data-bound UIs ARCHITECTURAL UI pattern KIND

IV.04 MVI (Model-View-Intent) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Unidirectional cycle: the View emits Intents, a reducer produces a new immutable Model (state), and the View renders that state. A single source of truth and one-way data flow make UI state predictable and reproducible. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Inconsistent UI state and hard-to-trace updates in MVVM with many mutable fields. Inspired by Redux and Cycle.js and adopted for complex Android and web UIs. Intent → Model (reducer) → View in a one-way cycle Client Service / component Module Domain core External system Sync call How it works The user acts; the view converts it into an Intent. The intent is passed to the model layer. A reducer combines the intent and current state into a new immutable state. Side effects (API calls) run and return results as new intents. The view renders the full state. State history can be logged or replayed for debugging. MVI (MODEL-VIEW-INTENT) Advantages Disadvantages Predictable, single source of truth. Boilerplate for intents, states and reducers. + Easy debugging, logging and replay. Large states can be costly to copy and render. Eliminates inconsistent partial updates. Steeper learning curve. Fits reactive and declarative UI. Overkill for simple screens. When to use When not to use Complex, state-heavy UIs such as editors, dashboards and forms with many interactions. Simple screens and content pages. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Compose-based Android apps Complex trading dashboards Keep state immutable and serializable. Model side effects explicitly. Use state snapshots for time-travel debugging. Collaborative editors. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Unidirectional immutable-state UI COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Complex stateful UIs MAIN DRAWBACK Boilerplate and state-size cost ARCHITECTURAL KIND UI pattern

IV.05 MVVM-C (MVVM with Coordinators) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA MVVM extended with Coordinators that own navigation and flow between screens, so ViewModels and views do not know about each other. Extract navigation responsibility into coordinator objects that create and present screens. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED View controllers or screens that hard-code navigation and become coupled to their neighbors. Popularized in iOS (Soroush Khanlou) to decouple navigation from view controllers. Coordinator creates screens and handles flow Domain core Service / component Sync call Async / event How it works The app starts a coordinator that builds the first screen. The coordinator creates the view and its ViewModel and injects dependencies. The view binds to the ViewModel as in MVVM. On a navigation event, the ViewModel signals the coordinator. The coordinator creates and presents the next screen. Child coordinators manage sub-flows and return control on finish. MVVM-C (MVVM WITH COORDINATORS) Advantages Disadvantages Screens are decoupled and reusable. Additional layer and boilerplate. + Navigation is centralized and testable. Coordinator lifecycle management complexity. Simplifies deep links and flow changes. Overkill for few-screen apps. Smaller views and ViewModels. Needs conventions for communication. When to use When not to use Mobile apps with multi-step flows, deep links and reusable screens. Small apps with simple linear navigation. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations iOS apps with onboarding and checkout flows Banking mobile apps. Keep coordinators free of business logic. Use delegation or events for results. Test flows by driving coordinators with fake screens. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE MVVM plus explicit navigation flow control COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Multi-flow mobile apps MAIN DRAWBACK Extra layer and coordinator lifecycle ARCHITECTURAL KIND UI pattern

IV.06 Component-Based UI Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA UIs built from encapsulated, reusable components that manage their own state and render from props, composed into a tree. Compose complex interfaces from small selfcontained pieces with explicit inputs and outputs. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Page-sized templates with global scripts and duplicated markup. React, Vue and Angular popularized composition of components with a virtual DOM or reactive rendering. Component tree; props flow down, events flow up Domain core Service / component Sync call Async / event How it works The UI is decomposed into a tree of components. Parents pass data to children as props. Components hold local state when needed. User events bubble up through callbacks. State changes trigger a re-render of affected components. Shared concerns use context or a global store. COMPONENT-BASED UI ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Reuse and consistency through a component library. Prop drilling and state management complexity. + Clear data flow and encapsulation. Over-fragmentation into tiny components. Testable in isolation (Storybook, unit tests). Performance pitfalls with unnecessary re-renders. Scales with teams and design systems. Framework lock-in. When to use When not to use Nearly all modern web and mobile UIs. Static pages without interactivity. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations React / Angular / Vue applications Design systems Keep components small and pure. Lift state sparingly. Use a design system and visual regression tests. Memoize expensive renders. Flutter widgets. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Compose UI from reusable components COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Interactive web and mobile UIs MAIN DRAWBACK Prop drilling and re-render cost ARCHITECTURAL KIND UI pattern

IV.07 Flux Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A unidirectional data flow pattern where Actions are dispatched to Stores through a central Dispatcher, and Views re-render from Store state. Data flows in a single direction — Action → Dispatcher Store → View — preventing cascading, hard-totrace updates. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Complex two-way data binding that made large client apps unpredictable. Facebook introduced Flux (2014) to fix cascading update bugs, such as the notification-count problem, in large React apps. Strict one-way flow with a central dispatcher Client Service / component Module Infrastructure Domain core External system Sync call Async / event How it works A user interaction in a view calls an action creator. The action creator creates an action and sends it to the dispatcher. The dispatcher forwards the action to all registered stores. Stores update their state and emit a change event. Views listening to stores read new state and re-render. Data never flows backward from views to stores directly. I V.07 FLUX ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Predictable one-way data flow. Boilerplate for actions and dispatcher wiring. + Easier debugging of state changes. Multiple stores can interdepend. Clear separation of concerns. Learning curve for newcomers. Scales to large applications. Largely superseded by Redux-style libraries. When to use When not to use Large client applications with complex shared state, as the concept behind many modern libraries. Small apps where local component state suffices. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Facebook’s original React app Early React applications. Keep stores free of side effects. Use action types and payload conventions. Prefer maintained libraries (Redux, Zustand) in new code. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE One-way flow via dispatcher and stores COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium–High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Predictable client state MAIN DRAWBACK Boilerplate; largely superseded ARCHITECTURAL KIND UI pattern

IV.08 Redux Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A single global store holding all application state, updated only by dispatching actions processed by pure reducer functions. Predictable state container: state is read-only, changes are described by actions, and reducers compute new state. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Scattered mutable state and unpredictability in large client applications. Dan Abramov and Andrew Clark simplified Flux (2015) into a single store with pure reducers and time-travel debugging. Single store, actions, reducers and middleware Service / component Module Infrastructure Domain core Database / store External system Sync call How it works A component dispatches an action describing what happened. Middleware may intercept it to run async side effects. The reducer computes new state from the previous state and action. The store saves the new immutable state. Subscribed components select the slices they need. DevTools can log and replay actions (time-travel). REDUX ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Predictable and debuggable state with a single source of truth. Boilerplate (reduced by Redux Toolkit). Overkill for local or small state. + Time-travel debugging and easy persistence. Indirection for async flows. + Testable pure reducers. Large state trees need normalization. + Rich ecosystem and tooling. When to use When not to use Large applications with complex shared state, undo/redo and advanced debugging needs. Small apps, or when server-state libraries (React Query) handle most state. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Large React SPAs Trading dashboards Normalize state, use selectors, split reducers by feature, and use Redux Toolkit. Keep server cache separate. Admin consoles. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Single store with pure reducers COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Complex shared client state MAIN DRAWBACK Boilerplate and indirection ARCHITECTURAL KIND UI pattern

UI PRINCIPLE IV.09 Unidirectional Data Flow Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A general principle where data flows in one direction state to view, events to state changes — rather than in loops of two-way bindings. State flows down to views; user intent flows up as events; only one place mutates state. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Hard-to-trace updates and inconsistent state from bidirectional updates. It is the common root of Flux, Redux, MVI, Elm and React’s props/state model. State flows down; events flow up; one update path Database / store Service / component Client Module Domain core Sync call How it works State is held in one place. The view is a pure function of state. The user interacts, producing an event. The event goes to an update function, never directly to the view or state. The update function produces the next state. The view re-renders from the new state. UNIDIRECTIONAL DATA FLOW ARCHITECTURE UI PRINCIPLE Advantages Disadvantages Predictable data flow and fewer bugs. Boilerplate for simple interactions. + Easy to test and reason about. Can feel indirect for small features. Enables replay, logging and time travel. Needs discipline for local vs global state. Works across frameworks. Large state updates can be expensive. When to use When not to use Any UI with non-trivial state; the default mental model in modern frameworks. Trivial widgets where local mutable state is simpler. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations React + Redux Keep views pure. Make updates explicit and serializable. Separate server state from UI state. Elm architecture Jetpack Compose MVI. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE One-way flow of state and events COMPLEXITY Low–Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Complex or shared UI state MAIN DRAWBACK Boilerplate for simple cases ARCHITECTURAL KIND UI principle
