V.01 API Gateway Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A single entry point that routes, secures and shapes client traffic to backend services. Centralize cross-cutting edge concerns — authentication, rate limiting, routing, TLS — so services stay focused on business logic. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Clients calling many services directly, duplicating security and policy logic and coupling to internal topology. Microservices multiplied endpoints; clients needed one stable, secure facade. Gateway applies edge policies and routes to services Client Infrastructure Service / component Sync call Async / event How it works The client sends a request to the gateway through the CDN/WAF. The gateway authenticates the token and applies rate limits. It resolves the target service via discovery. It routes the request, applying retries and circuit breaking. It may aggregate, transform or cache the response. It emits metrics, logs and trace headers for observability. API GATEWAY ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Single secure entry point and consistent policies. Potential bottleneck and single point of failure. + Hides internal topology from clients. Risk of becoming a “smart” monolith with business + Offloads auth, TLS, throttling and caching. logic. + Enables protocol translation and versioning. Extra hop and operational burden. Requires scaling and HA design. When to use When not to use Microservices exposed to external clients, mobile backends and API products needing centralized security and policy. A single service or purely internal service-to-service traffic (use a mesh for east-west). Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spring Cloud Gateway / Kong / AWS API Gateway in front of services Public API platforms Deploy multiple stateless gateway instances. Keep business logic out. Define timeouts and circuit breakers per route. See API Gateway vs Service Mesh (Part IX). Mobile backends. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Central edge entry and policy enforcement COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE External APIs over many services MAIN DRAWBACK Bottleneck and logic creep risk ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

V.02 Service Mesh Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A dedicated infrastructure layer of sidecar proxies that handles service-to-service communication — mTLS, retries, routing and telemetry. Move networking concerns out of application code into a transparent proxy layer managed by a central control plane. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Duplicated resilience, security and observability logic across many services and languages. Polyglot microservice fleets needed uniform eastwest traffic control (Istio, Linkerd, Envoy). Data plane sidecars controlled by a control plane Infrastructure Service / component Sync call Async / event How it works Each service pod runs with a sidecar proxy. All inbound and outbound traffic passes through the proxy. The control plane pushes routing rules, policies and certificates. Proxies establish mTLS and apply retries, timeouts and circuit breaking. Traffic shifting enables canary and blue/green releases. Proxies emit uniform metrics, logs and traces. SERVICE MESH ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Uniform security, resilience and observability without code changes. Added latency and resource overhead per pod. Significant operational complexity. + Language-agnostic. Steep learning curve and debugging difficulty. + Fine-grained traffic control and canary releases. Overkill for a small number of services. + Zero-trust service identity via mTLS. When to use When not to use Large Kubernetes microservice estates needing mTLS, traffic policies and consistent observability. Small systems with few services, or teams lacking platform maturity. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Istio or Linkerd on Kubernetes Zero-trust service meshes in banks Adopt incrementally by namespace. Budget CPU and memory for proxies. Standardize on tracing headers. Consider ambient mesh to reduce sidecar cost. Canary-release platforms. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Platform layer for service-to-service traffic COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Large polyglot Kubernetes fleets MAIN DRAWBACK Operational complexity and overhead ARCHITECTURAL KIND Infrastructure pattern

V.03 Sidecar Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A helper container deployed alongside the main application container, sharing its lifecycle and network namespace to provide supporting capabilities. Attach cross-cutting functionality (logging, proxy, config) as a separate process, not as a library. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Embedding polyglot cross-cutting concerns into every application. Containers and pods made co-located helper processes cheap, isolated and independently versioned. Sidecar and application share a pod Service / component Infrastructure External system Sync call How it works The pod starts the app container and its sidecar together. They share network namespace and volumes. The app talks to the sidecar over localhost. The sidecar handles a cross-cutting function (proxying, logging, secrets). The sidecar communicates with external systems on the app’s behalf. Both scale and restart together as one unit. SIDECAR ARCHITECTURE Advantages Language-agnostic reuse of cross-cutting logic. + Isolation from application code. Independent upgrades of helper functionality. Keeps applications simple. When to use Service mesh proxies, log/metric agents, config and secret syncers, and legacy integration shims. Real-world applications Envoy proxy sidecars Fluent Bit log shippers Dapr runtime Vault agent. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Co-located helper process SCALABILITY High COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Per-pod resource overhead Disadvantages Extra resource consumption per instance. Lifecycle and startup-ordering complexity. Added network hop and debugging surface. Many sidecars multiply operational overhead. When not to use When a shared library is simpler and the system is single-language. Key engineering considerations Set resource limits for sidecars. Order startup and shutdown explicitly. Monitor sidecar health along with the app. COMPLEXITY Low–Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Cross-cutting capabilities in containers ARCHITECTURAL Deployment pattern KIND

V.04 Ambassador Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A helper proxy deployed next to a client application to handle outbound network concerns — retries, circuit breaking, routing and monitoring. Offload client-side connectivity logic to an out-ofprocess proxy so the application stays unaware of the network’s complexity. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Legacy or polyglot clients lacking resilience features for talking to remote services. Often used to modernize legacy apps without modifying their code. Ambassador proxies outbound calls on behalf of the client Service / component Infrastructure External system Sync call Async / event How it works The client sends requests to the ambassador on localhost. The ambassador resolves the remote service and sets up TLS. It applies retries, timeouts and circuit breaking. It forwards the request and returns the response. It records metrics and logs for outbound traffic. The client remains unchanged. AMBASSADOR ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Adds resilience to clients without code changes. Extra hop and resource usage. + Centralizes client-side networking logic. Operational overhead per client. Keeps legacy apps compatible with modern backends. Overlaps with sidecar and mesh; unclear roles. Configuration must stay in sync. + Language independent. When to use When not to use Modernizing legacy clients, enforcing consistent outbound policies, and migration scenarios. Greenfield systems already using a service mesh or resilient client libraries. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Legacy app connecting to cloud APIs Database proxies handling connection pooling and TLS. Treat as a specialization of sidecar focused on outbound calls. Monitor ambassador latency and failures. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Out-of-process client-side proxy COMPLEXITY Low–Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Legacy client modernization MAIN DRAWBACK Extra hop and overlap with mesh ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment pattern

MIGRATION PATTERN V.05 Strangler Fig Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Incrementally replace a legacy system by routing functionality to new services behind a facade until the old system can be retired. Grow the new system around the old one, one slice at a time, instead of a risky big-bang rewrite. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED High-risk rewrites of legacy systems that cannot be paused or replaced all at once. Martin Fowler named it after strangler figs that gradually envelop host trees. A routing facade shifts traffic from legacy to new services Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Place a facade or proxy in front of the legacy system. Pick one capability and build it as a new service. Route that capability’s traffic to the new service. Synchronize or migrate the relevant data. Repeat until the legacy system has no remaining responsibilities. Decommission the legacy system. STRANGLER FIG ARCHITECTURE MIGRATION PATTERN Advantages Disadvantages Incremental, low-risk migration. + Value delivered early and continuously. Long-running dual systems and data synchronization. + Easy rollback by changing routes. Facade can become a bottleneck. + Legacy keeps running during the transition. Needs careful seam identification. Risk of never finishing the migration. When to use When not to use Replacing or modernizing legacy monoliths while they remain in production. Small systems where a rewrite is cheaper, or when no clean seams exist. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Monolith-to-microservices migrations Mainframe modernization Choose seams along business capabilities. Use CDC for data sync. Keep migration metrics and an explicit end date. Plan data ownership transfer. Platform replacements in banks. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Incremental legacy replacement COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium — temporary BEST USE CASE Legacy modernization MAIN DRAWBACK Long dual-running period ARCHITECTURAL KIND Migration pattern

V.06 Database-per-Service Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Each microservice owns its private database, and other services access that data only through the owning service’s API or events. Data ownership defines service autonomy: no shared tables, no cross-service joins. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Hidden coupling through shared schemas that block independent deployment and evolution. A shared database turns microservices into a distributed monolith; private data enables independent change. Each service has its own datastore; sharing happens through APIs and events Service / component Database / store Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works Each service chooses the datastore that fits its workload. Only the owning service reads and writes its data. Other services request data through the owner’s API. State changes are published as events. Consumers keep their own local copies (read models) if needed. Cross-service consistency is handled through sagas. DATABASE-PER-SERVICE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Loose coupling and independent schema evolution. No joins or ACID transactions across services. + Freedom to pick the right datastore per service. Data duplication and eventual consistency. Independent scaling and failure isolation. Reporting across services is harder. Clear data ownership. More databases to operate. When to use When not to use Microservices needing autonomy, polyglot persistence, and independent releases. Small systems or tightly related data that always changes together. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations E-commerce platforms with separate orders, catalog and customer stores Use sagas and events for consistency, CDC or an analytics store for reporting, and treat schemas as private. See Shared Database (this part). Fintech services with isolated ledgers. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Private data per service COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Autonomous microservices MAIN DRAWBACK Distributed data consistency ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

V.07 Shared Database Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Multiple services or applications read and write the same database schema. A common data store is the integration mechanism, giving simple joins and transactions across components. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED The complexity of data synchronization and distributed transactions during early decomposition. Legacy integration and simple systems often start here; it is easy and consistent. Several services coupled through one schema Service / component Database / store External system Sync call Dependency direction How it works Services connect directly to the shared database. Each reads and writes tables as needed. ACID transactions span tables from multiple components. A schema change affects every service using it. Deployments must be coordinated around schema versions. Performance contention and locks affect all consumers. V.07 SHARED DATABASE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Simple integration and joins. + Strong consistency via local ACID transactions. Tight coupling through the schema; coordinated releases. + Easy reporting and querying. Contention and a single scaling bottleneck. + Quick to implement. Unclear ownership of data and rules. Blocks independent technology choices. When to use When not to use Small systems, a transitional step in migrations, or tightly related legacy applications. Independent teams and services needing autonomy and independent deployment. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Legacy ERP integrations Reporting directly on OLTP If used, restrict write access by table ownership, use views or APIs for access, and plan to split. Treat as technical debt in microservices. Early-stage service splits. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Integration through a common schema COMPLEXITY Low SCALABILITY Low–Medium MAINTAINABILITY Low COUPLING Very high BEST USE CASE Simple or transitional systems MAIN DRAWBACK Schema coupling blocks autonomy ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

V.08 API Composition / Aggregator Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A composer service queries multiple services and combines their results into one response; the Aggregator pattern is the same idea applied at the service level. Implement cross-service queries by calling owners and joining in memory instead of joining in the database. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Queries spanning data owned by several services under database-per-service. Without shared databases, joins move into a composition layer. Composer fans out to services and merges results Client Service / component Sync call How it works The client asks the composer for a composite view. The composer calls the owning services, in parallel where possible. It applies timeouts, retries and fallbacks per call. It joins and filters the results in memory. It returns the composed response. Partial failures yield degraded or cached responses. API COMPOSITION / AGGREGATOR ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Simple way to answer cross-service queries. Latency of the slowest dependency. + Keeps data ownership intact. In-memory joins are inefficient for large data. Parallel calls reduce latency. Reduced availability if dependencies fail. Fewer client round trips. No transactional consistency across calls. When to use When not to use Moderate-sized composite queries for dashboards, detail pages and BFFs. Large joins and heavy reporting (use CQRS or a data warehouse). Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Order detail pages Mobile home screens Fan out concurrently with timeouts and bulkheads. Cache stable data. Provide fallbacks. Use CQRS read models if queries get heavy. Customer 360 views. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Compose data from multiple services SCALABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium MAIN DRAWBACK Latency and availability coupling COMPLEXITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Cross-service reads ARCHITECTURAL Architectural pattern KIND

V.09 Fan-Out / Fan-In Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Work is split into many parallel tasks (fan-out) and the results are collected and combined (fan-in). Parallelize independent work to cut latency or increase throughput, then aggregate. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Long-running sequential processing of independent units of work. Elastic compute makes parallel decomposition cheap; MapReduce popularized the idea. Splitter distributes tasks; aggregator joins results Client Service / component Queue / broker Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works A coordinator splits a job into independent tasks. Tasks are placed on a queue or invoked in parallel. Workers process tasks concurrently and report results. An aggregator collects results and tracks completion. Failed or slow tasks are retried or timed out. The merged result is stored or returned. FAN-OUT / FAN-IN ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Reduced total latency via parallelism. Aggregation and completion tracking complexity. + Scales with the number of workers. Stragglers delay the total result. Natural fit for serverless and queues. Partial failure handling is required. Fault isolation per task. Resource spikes and downstream overload. When to use When not to use Batch jobs, document or image processing, scattergather queries, and map/reduce style computation. Strictly sequential dependent steps or tiny tasks where overhead dominates. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Video transcoding by chunks Search across shards Make tasks idempotent. Set concurrency limits and timeouts. Track completion with counters or durable workflows. Handle partial results explicitly. Multi-provider price comparison. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Parallel split and join COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Parallelizable batch and query work MAIN DRAWBACK Coordination and straggler handling ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

V.10 Distributed Transaction Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Coordinating a transaction across multiple resources or services, classically with two-phase commit (2PC), so all commit or all abort. A coordinator asks all participants to prepare; if every one agrees, it instructs them to commit, otherwise abort. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Atomic updates across multiple databases or resource managers. Enterprise systems (XA, JTA) needed atomicity across databases and message brokers. Two-phase commit with a coordinator Client Domain core How it works The application starts a transaction with a coordinator. Participants perform work and lock resources. Phase 1: the coordinator asks each to prepare and collects votes. If all vote yes, Phase 2 instructs everyone to commit. If any votes no or times out, everyone rolls back. The coordinator logs decisions to recover from crashes. DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Strong atomicity and consistency. + Familiar semantics (ACID) across resources. Blocking: locks held across the network; coordinator failure stalls. + Standard support (XA, JTA). Poor availability and throughput at scale. + Simple application programming model. Not supported by most NoSQL and cloud services. Tight coupling between participants. When to use When not to use Few trusted resources inside one datacenter where strong atomicity is mandatory. Microservices at scale, cross-organization calls or high-availability systems — use sagas. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Banking systems with XA across databases Legacy JTA applications. Keep transactions short. Prefer idempotent sagas or the outbox pattern in microservices. Monitor in-doubt transactions and coordinator recovery. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Atomic commit across resources COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Low MAINTAINABILITY Low COUPLING Very high BEST USE CASE Strict atomicity across few resources MAIN DRAWBACK Blocking and poor availability ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

V.11 Event-Driven Microservices WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Microservices that collaborate through events on a broker, each reacting to facts and keeping local read models. Combine service autonomy with asynchronous event flow for loose coupling and resilience. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Synchronous call chains that couple availability and latency across services. Event backbones such as Kafka made reliable asynchronous integration practical at scale. Service / component Database / store Infrastructure Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works A service commits state and an outbox record in one local transaction. A relay (CDC) publishes the record to Kafka. Subscribers consume the event at their own pace. Each updates its local data or triggers new events. Failures use retries, DLQs and idempotent handlers. Event schemas are versioned in a registry. EVENT-DRIVEN MICROSERVICES Advantages Disadvantages Loose coupling and independent scaling. Eventual consistency and complex debugging. + Resilience: consumers can be down temporarily. Needs idempotency, ordering and schema + Easy to add new consumers. governance. + Audit trail and replay. Duplicate and out-of-order events. Broker operations. When to use When not to use Complex domains with many reactions to changes, real-time integration and high-scale systems. Simple CRUD or low-latency synchronous workflows. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations E-commerce order pipelines Payment and ledger platforms Use the transactional outbox. Version schemas. Handle duplicates with idempotency keys. Instrument with correlation IDs and distributed tracing. Ride-hailing dispatch. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Autonomous services collaborating via events COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Real-time, loosely coupled systems MAIN DRAWBACK Eventual consistency and traceability ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

V.12 Multi-Tenant Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A single software deployment serves multiple customers (tenants) while isolating their data, configuration and performance. Share infrastructure to gain efficiency, with explicit tenant isolation in data, compute and security. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED The cost and operational overhead of running a separate stack per customer. SaaS economics depend on shared, centrally operated platforms. Shared application tier with pooled, bridged or siloed data isolation Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call How it works A request arrives with a tenant identifier (subdomain, token claim). The gateway resolves and propagates tenant context. Services enforce tenant filters on every data access. Data is stored in pooled, schema-per-tenant or dedicated stores. Rate limits and quotas protect tenants from noisy neighbors. Billing and metrics are attributed per tenant. MULTI-TENANT ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Cost efficiency and simple operations. + Fast onboarding of new tenants. Noisy neighbors and cross-tenant data leakage risks. + Single codebase and release for all. Complex tenant-aware security and data management. + Flexible isolation tiers per plan. Per-tenant customization is difficult. Blast radius covers all tenants. When to use When not to use SaaS products with many customers, where cost and operational efficiency matter. Customers requiring strict physical isolation or very heterogeneous deployments (consider single-tenant or cells). Real-world applications Key engineering considerations CRM and HR SaaS platforms Collaboration tools Enforce tenant context centrally and add row-level security. Test isolation continuously. Offer tiered isolation. Combine with cells to limit blast radius. Fintech platforms serving multiple banks. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Shared platform with tenant isolation COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE SaaS with many customers MAIN DRAWBACK Isolation risk and noisy neighbors ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural pattern

V.13 Cell-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA The system is split into independent, identical cells, each a complete stack serving a subset of users or tenants, behind a thin routing layer. Limit blast radius: a failure or bad deployment affects only one cell’s share of users. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Large-scale outages caused by shared components and cascading failures. Used at AWS and Slack to contain failures and scale by adding cells rather than growing shared services. A router assigns users to isolated cells Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call How it works A router maps each user or tenant to a cell. Requests go to the assigned cell and are served entirely within it. Cells share nothing at runtime, including data. A failure or bad release is contained to one cell. New capacity is added by creating new cells. Releases roll out cell by cell. CELL-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Strongly limited blast radius. Complex routing and cell assignment management. + Predictable capacity and easy scaling by replication. Cross-cell operations are hard. Safer progressive deployment. Duplicated infrastructure cost. Simpler capacity planning per cell. Rebalancing users between cells is complex. When to use When not to use Large-scale, high-availability platforms where outage containment is critical. Small systems or those needing heavy cross-user data interaction. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations AWS and Slack cell architectures Large SaaS and payments platforms. Keep the router thin and highly available. Define cell size by a capacity unit. Automate cell provisioning and per-cell observability. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Isolated, identical stacks per user group SCALABILITY Very high COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Routing complexity and duplicated cost COMPLEXITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium–High BEST USE CASE Outage containment at scale ARCHITECTURAL Deployment topology KIND

V.14 Federated Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Autonomous systems or domains cooperate under shared standards and a thin federation layer, retaining independent ownership. Provide a unified experience or governance across independent subsystems without centralizing them. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Integrating separately owned systems (business units, organizations) while preserving autonomy. Large organizations and ecosystems cannot centralize everything; GraphQL federation and federated identity address this. A federation gateway composes independently owned subgraphs Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call How it works Each domain owns its service, data and schema. Domains publish their contracts to a registry. A federation layer composes them into a unified API or identity. Requests are planned and routed across domains. Shared standards (auth, naming, SLOs) ensure interoperability. Domains evolve independently within agreed contracts. FEDERATED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Domain autonomy with unified access. Governance and standards overhead. + Scales organizationally. Cross-domain performance and consistency + Gradual integration of heterogeneous systems. challenges. + Clear ownership. Gateway complexity. Harder end-to-end debugging. When to use When not to use Multi-team or multi-organization platforms needing a unified interface, such as GraphQL federation and federated identity. Small organizations or systems that can be simply centralized. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Apollo GraphQL Federation Federated SSO between enterprises Define global standards sparingly and enforce them with automation. Version contracts and monitor crossdomain latency. Open banking ecosystems. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Unify autonomous domains under standards COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low–Medium BEST USE CASE Multi-team platforms and ecosystems MAIN DRAWBACK Governance and cross-domain complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

V.15 Multi-Region Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA An application deployed in multiple geographic regions for lower latency, higher availability and data residency compliance. Place services and data near users and survive the loss of an entire region. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Latency for global users, regional outages, and regulatory data residency. Global products and critical systems cannot rely on a single region. Global traffic routing across regions with cross-region replication Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works DNS or global load balancing routes users to the nearest healthy region. Each region runs a full application stack. Data is replicated across regions asynchronously or synchronously. Health checks detect regional failure. Traffic fails over to another region. Writes follow a regional-primary or multi-primary strategy. MULTI-REGION ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Lower latency for global users. Data consistency and replication lag complexity. + Survives region-level failures. Higher cost and operational overhead. Meets data residency requirements. Conflict resolution for multi-writer data. Enables regional maintenance and rollout. Testing failover is hard. When to use When not to use Global user bases, high availability targets, or regulatory requirements. Regional products with relaxed availability needs. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Global e-commerce Streaming platforms Banking systems with disaster recovery regions. Define RPO/RTO per dataset. Choose consistency model carefully. Test failover regularly. Keep configuration and secrets synchronized. See Active- Active vs Active-Passive. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Deploy across geographic regions COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Global, highly available systems MAIN DRAWBACK Data consistency and cost ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment topology

V.16 Active-Active Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Two or more sites serve production traffic simultaneously, each capable of taking over the others’ load. Use all capacity all the time and remove failover delay by distributing live traffic across sites. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Idle standby capacity and slow failover in activepassive designs. Always-on services need near-zero downtime and efficient resource use. Both regions serve traffic with bidirectional data replication Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works A global load balancer splits traffic across regions. Each region reads and writes its local data store. Changes replicate between regions in both directions. Conflicts are resolved by policy (last-write-wins, CRDTs, partitioning). If a region fails, the load balancer shifts all traffic to survivors. Surviving regions must have capacity headroom. ACTIVE-ACTIVE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Near-zero failover time and no idle capacity. Conflict resolution and complex data consistency. + Lower latency by serving locally. Capacity planning for failover headroom. Horizontal capacity across sites. Higher design and operational complexity. Continuous validation of every site. Possible split-brain. When to use When not to use Global always-on services with tolerance for eventual consistency or partitionable data. Systems requiring strict global consistency or with limited ops maturity. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Global SaaS platforms Content and social platforms DynamoDB Global Tables workloads. Partition data by owner region to avoid conflicts. Design idempotent writes. Reserve failover headroom. Test region failure regularly. See Active-Active vs Active-Passive (Part IX). Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE All sites serve live traffic COMPLEXITY Very high SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Always-on global systems MAIN DRAWBACK Data conflicts and complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment topology

V.17 Active-Passive Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA One site serves production traffic while a standby site is kept ready to take over on failure. Simplify consistency by keeping a single writer while maintaining a replicated warm or cold standby for recovery. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Availability and disaster recovery without the complexity of multi-writer data. It is simpler, cheaper to reason about, and often adequate for RTO/RPO targets. Traffic goes to the primary; the standby takes over on failover Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Users are routed only to the primary site. Data replicates continuously to the standby. Health checks monitor the primary. On failure, the standby replica is promoted. DNS or load balancer switches traffic to the standby. After recovery, the primary is rebuilt and failback occurs. ACTIVE-PASSIVE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Simple consistency with a single writer. + Lower cost than active-active, especially with a cold Failover takes time (RTO) and may lose recent data (RPO). or warm standby. Standby capacity is idle or underused. Easier to operate and reason about. Failover paths are rarely exercised and may fail. + Clear failover procedure. Failback is risky. When to use When not to use Systems with moderate RTO/RPO targets and strict consistency requirements. Zero-downtime or global low-latency requirements. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Enterprise databases with standby Core banking DR Automate failover and test it regularly with game days. Monitor replication lag and define RPO. Rehearse failback. Internal business applications. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE One active site, one standby COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Strong consistency with DR MAIN DRAWBACK Failover delay and unused standby ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment topology

VI.01 Database-Centric Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A design where the shared relational database is the system’s center: business logic, integrity and often integration live in or around the database. Centralize data and enforce rules close to it with constraints, stored procedures and views so every application sees one consistent truth. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Inconsistent data across applications and duplicated validation logic. Relational databases offered strong integrity and tooling; many enterprises integrated applications through one schema. Multiple applications integrated through one central database Client Database / store Infrastructure Sync call How it works Applications connect to the central database. Business rules run as constraints, triggers or stored procedures. Applications access data through views and procedures. The database enforces integrity and transactions. Reports and integrations read directly from the same schema. Schema changes are coordinated across all consumers. DATABASE-CENTRIC ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Strong data integrity and a single source of truth. Tight coupling through the schema. + Mature tooling, ACID and fast set-based operations. Database becomes a scaling and change + Simple integration and reporting. bottleneck. + Logic close to data reduces round trips. Business logic in SQL is hard to test and version. Vendor lock-in. When to use When not to use Data-intensive back-office systems with strong consistency needs and few independent teams. Microservices or teams needing independent deployment and polyglot data. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Legacy ERP Banking core systems on stored procedures Reporting-centric platforms. Control access through views and procedures. Version schema with migrations (Flyway/Liquibase). Isolate reporting on replicas. Treat as a stepping stone before splitting by service. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE The database is the system’s center COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Low–Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING High BEST USE CASE Integrity-critical back-office systems MAIN DRAWBACK Schema coupling and scaling limits ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

VI.02 Polyglot Persistence WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Using multiple data store technologies, each chosen for the data model and access pattern of the workload it serves. No single database is best for everything; match store to need — relational, document, key-value, graph, search. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Forcing every workload into one database that fits none perfectly. NoSQL and specialized stores matured, and microservices allowed independent data choices. Different stores for different workloads How it works Identify workloads and their access patterns. Select a store per workload (ACID, document, cache, search, graph). Services access the stores they own. Changes flow between stores via events or CDC. Search and analytic stores are derived from the source of truth. Operations standardize backup, monitoring and security across stores. POLYGLOT PERSISTENCE Advantages Disadvantages Best performance and fit per workload. Operational burden of many technologies. + Independent scaling of each store. Data consistency across stores is hard. Features unavailable in a single database. Skills and tooling fragmentation. Avoids over-stretching one technology. Cross-store queries are difficult. When to use When not to use Systems with distinct workloads, such as transactions, search, caching and recommendations, and teams able to operate them. Small teams or workloads that fit comfortably in PostgreSQL. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations E-commerce (SQL orders, document catalog, search index) Designate one source of truth per dataset. Use CDC to feed derived stores. Limit the number of technologies and standardize operations. Social networks with graph and cache Fintech with ledger and analytics. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Right store for each workload COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Diverse access patterns MAIN DRAWBACK Operational and consistency overhead ARCHITECTURAL KIND Data architecture

VI.03 Data Lake Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A central repository storing raw data of any format at scale in cheap object storage, structured later on read (schema-on-read). Ingest everything first, model later, and let many engines analyze the same raw data. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Rigid warehouse schemas that cannot absorb diverse, high-volume or unstructured data. Hadoop and cloud object storage made storing all data cheap and flexible. External system Infrastructure Database / store Service / component Client Sync call Async / event How it works Data from many sources is ingested as-is into the raw zone. Files are stored in open formats (Parquet, JSON, ORC). Processing jobs clean and standardize data into curated zones. A catalog tracks schemas, lineage and access. Engines like Spark and Presto query data on demand. Data scientists and BI tools consume curated datasets. DATA LAKE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Cheap, scalable storage for any data type. Risk of a “data swamp” without governance. + Flexibility: schema-on-read and many engines. Weak ACID and consistency for updates. Supports ML and exploratory analytics. + Preserves raw history. Performance and quality depend on layout and tooling. Security and access control are complex. When to use When not to use Large, varied datasets, ML workloads and exploratory analytics. Pure BI with strict performance and governance needs (use a warehouse or lakehouse). Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Clickstream analytics ML feature stores Partition and compress (Parquet). Maintain a catalog and data quality checks. Define zone-based access. Consider table formats (Delta/Iceberg) for reliability. IoT telemetry archives. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Raw, flexible central data storage COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Low–Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Large varied data and ML MAIN DRAWBACK Governance risk (data swamp) ARCHITECTURAL KIND Data architecture

VI.04 Data Warehouse Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A central repository of structured, integrated, historical data modeled for analytics (schema-onwrite), typically with star schemas. Clean, model and integrate data before storing it so analysts get fast, consistent, trusted queries. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Slow, inconsistent reporting directly on operational systems. Inmon and Kimball methodologies separated analytics from OLTP; MPP and cloud warehouses scaled it. ETL into a modeled warehouse serving BI Database / store External system Infrastructure Client Sync call How it works Operational systems and files are extracted on a schedule. Data is cleansed, conformed and loaded into staging. It is transformed into facts and dimensions. The warehouse stores integrated historical data. Data marts expose subject-specific views. BI tools query the optimized models. DATA WAREHOUSE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Trusted, consistent, high-performance analytics. + Strong governance and data quality. Optimized for SQL and BI workloads. Historical tracking (slowly changing dimensions). When to use Enterprise reporting, KPIs and BI where trusted, structured data is needed. Real-world applications Financial reporting Retail sales analytics Snowflake / BigQuery / Redshift deployments. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Modeled, integrated analytics store SCALABILITY High COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Rigidity and modeling effort Disadvantages Rigid schemas and upfront modeling effort. Expensive for unstructured or very large raw data. Latency from ETL cycles. Costly to change. When not to use Raw unstructured data, exploratory ML, and lowlatency streaming (consider lake or lakehouse). Key engineering considerations Model dimensions carefully. Version transformations (dbt). Control cost with partitioning and clustering. Monitor data freshness. COMPLEXITY Medium–High MAINTAINABILITY Medium–High BEST USE CASE Trusted BI and reporting ARCHITECTURAL Data architecture KIND

VI.05 Lakehouse Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A single platform combining low-cost lake storage with warehouse features — ACID tables, schema enforcement, governance and SQL performance. Add a transactional table layer (Delta, Iceberg, Hudi) on object storage so one copy of data serves BI, ML and streaming. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Maintaining separate lakes and warehouses with duplicated data and pipelines. Open table formats brought reliability and performance to lake storage. One storage layer with a transactional table format serving all workloads External system Infrastructure Database / store Service / component Client Sync call How it works Data is ingested from batch and streaming sources. It is written as ACID tables on object storage. Table metadata enables schema enforcement and time travel. A catalog governs access and lineage. SQL engines serve BI; Spark and ML read the same tables. Optimizations such as compaction and clustering sustain performance. LAKEHOUSE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages One copy of data for BI, ML and streaming. + ACID, schema enforcement and time travel on cheap Younger ecosystem; tuning and compaction required. storage. BI performance may trail dedicated warehouses. Open formats reduce lock-in. Operational complexity of table maintenance. + Simplified architecture and governance. Migration effort. When to use When not to use Organizations wanting unified analytics and ML without duplicating lake and warehouse stacks. Small BI-only environments better served by a managed warehouse. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Databricks Delta Lake platforms Iceberg on S3 with Trino Choose one table format and catalog. Schedule compaction and vacuum jobs. Apply medallion layers. See Data Lake vs Warehouse vs Lakehouse (Part IX). Unified retail analytics. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Warehouse reliability on lake storage COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Unified BI + ML analytics MAIN DRAWBACK Table maintenance and maturity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Data architecture

VI.06 Data Mesh Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A decentralized approach where domain teams own and publish data as products, supported by a selfserve platform and federated governance. Treat data as a product owned by domains rather than a centralized team’s pipeline output. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Central data team bottlenecks and lack of domain context in large organizations. Zhamak Dehghani proposed it (2019) as data volumes and domains outgrew centralized lakes. Service / component Database / store Infrastructure Client Sync call Dependency direction How it works Domains own their operational and analytical data. Each domain publishes data products with contracts and SLAs. A self-serve platform provides tooling to build and run them. Products are discoverable through a catalog. Federated governance sets global standards and policies. Consumers combine products across domains. DATA MESH ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Scales data ownership with the organization. Needs organizational maturity and cultural change. + Domain context improves quality and relevance. Duplication of effort and inconsistent standards risk. Removes central team bottleneck. Platform investment required. Clear accountability and SLAs. Cross-domain integration complexity. When to use When not to use Large organizations with many domains and a central data bottleneck. Small companies or those without strong domain teams and platform capability. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Large banks and retailers with domain-aligned data products Define product contracts and quality SLOs. Invest in the platform first. Automate governance. Start with a few high-value products. Telecom analytics. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Domain-owned data products COMPLEXITY Very high SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Large multi-domain organizations MAIN DRAWBACK Organizational and platform prerequisites ARCHITECTURAL KIND Organizational data architecture

VI.07 Data Fabric Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A metadata-driven integration layer that connects data across distributed sources and automates discovery, governance and delivery. Use active metadata, knowledge graphs and automation to provide unified access without physically centralizing all data. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Fragmented data across clouds, databases and applications that is hard to find and integrate. Hybrid and multi-cloud estates made centralization impractical. A metadata-driven fabric layer virtualizes access across sources Database / store Infrastructure Client Sync call How it works Connectors catalog all data sources. Active metadata builds a knowledge graph of data and relationships. Virtualization exposes unified views without copying data. Governance and security policies apply uniformly. Automation recommends pipelines and data products. Consumers discover and query data through one layer. V I .07 DATA FABRIC ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Unified access across heterogeneous sources. Vendor- and tool-heavy; complex implementation. + Less data movement and duplication. Virtualized queries can be slow across networks. Automated governance and discovery. Quality still depends on source systems. Works in hybrid and multi-cloud environments. Metadata management is hard. When to use When not to use Enterprises with highly distributed data estates needing unified discovery and governance. Simple environments where one warehouse or lakehouse suffices. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Hybrid enterprises integrating on-prem and cloud Regulated organizations requiring lineage. Invest in metadata quality. Combine virtualization with selective replication for performance. See Data Mesh for the organizational counterpart. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Metadata-driven unified data access SCALABILITY High COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Tooling complexity and virtualization latency COMPLEXITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Hybrid, fragmented estates ARCHITECTURAL Data architecture KIND

VI.08 Medallion Architecture (Bronze, Silver, Gold) WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A layered lakehouse design that progressively refines data through Bronze (raw), Silver (cleansed) and Gold (business-ready) tables. Improve data quality in stages so each layer has a clear contract and consumers choose the right level. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Unstructured pipelines where raw and business-ready data are mixed, making quality and lineage unclear. Popularized by Databricks as a clean pattern for Delta Lake pipelines. Data refined through Bronze, Silver and Gold layers External system Database / store Client Sync call How it works Raw data lands unchanged in Bronze with metadata (source, load time). Silver jobs clean, deduplicate, validate and conform schemas. Gold jobs aggregate and model data for business use cases. Each layer is a set of versioned, ACID tables. Quality checks gate promotion between layers. Consumers read from Silver or Gold as appropriate. MEDALLION ARCHITECTURE (BRONZE, SILVER, GOLD) Advantages Disadvantages Clear separation of quality levels and lineage. Storage duplication across layers. + Reprocessing from Bronze is always possible. Pipeline sprawl without conventions. Incremental processing and easy debugging. Latency through multiple hops. Supports both BI and ML consumers. Not a substitute for governance. When to use When not to use Lakehouse analytics pipelines where data quality and traceability matter. Tiny datasets or purely transactional systems. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Retail analytics on Delta Lake Customer 360 pipelines Define layer contracts and quality gates. Use incremental processing and idempotent jobs. Track lineage and cost per layer. IoT telemetry refinement. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Layered progressive data refinement SCALABILITY High COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Storage duplication and pipeline sprawl COMPLEXITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY High BEST USE CASE Lakehouse pipelines ARCHITECTURAL Data architecture KIND

VI.09 Data Pipeline Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA An automated sequence of stages that ingests, transforms, validates and delivers data between systems, in batch or streaming mode. Treat data movement as software: orchestrated, tested, observable and idempotent. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Manual, brittle data transfers and inconsistent analytics inputs. Growing numbers of sources and consumers required reliable, repeatable data delivery. Ingest, process, store, serve with orchestration and monitoring External system Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Client Sync call Dependency direction How it works The orchestrator triggers or monitors each stage. Ingestion pulls or receives data from sources. Transformations clean, join and enrich the data. Results are loaded to the target stores. Quality checks validate outputs and alert on anomalies. Failed stages retry or rerun idempotently with lineage tracking. DATA PIPELINE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Reliable and repeatable data delivery. + Modular stages with observability. Operational complexity and dependency management. + Supports batch and streaming. Schema changes break downstream stages. + Enables data quality and lineage. Backfills and reprocessing are costly. Pipeline sprawl without ownership. When to use When not to use Any analytics, ML or integration platform moving data between systems. One-off transfers where a manual script suffices. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Daily revenue pipelines ML feature pipelines Make every task idempotent. Version schemas. Add data contracts and freshness alerts. Monitor SLAs and cost. CDC to warehouse. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Orchestrated multi-stage data movement COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Reliable data delivery MAIN DRAWBACK Dependency and schema fragility ARCHITECTURAL KIND Data architecture

VI.10 ETL / ELT Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA ETL transforms data before loading into the target; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the target system. ELT exploits scalable warehouse and lake compute for transformation, while ETL cleanses data in a separate engine before storage. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Moving data from operational sources to analytics stores with the right transformation placement. Cheap, scalable cloud warehouses shifted heavy transformation into the destination. ETL transforms before load; ELT transforms after load Database / store Service / component Sync call How it works Extract data from sources, usually incrementally. ETL: transform in a separate engine, then load clean data. ELT: load raw data to the target first. ELT: run SQL transformations inside the warehouse or lakehouse. Both validate and document transformations. Schedule and monitor runs; support reprocessing. ETL / ELT ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages ETL: strict control, smaller targets, sensitive data filtered early. ETL needs separate compute and slows change. ELT stores raw (possibly sensitive) data in the + ELT: faster loading and scalable transformation. target. ELT keeps raw data for reprocessing. ELT transformations can raise warehouse costs. + Both are well-understood patterns with mature tools. Both require careful dependency management. When to use When not to use ETL for compliance-driven pre-load cleansing; ELT for cloud warehouses and lakehouses with flexible analytics. ELT where raw sensitive data must not land in the target. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Informatica ETL pipelines Fivetran + dbt ELT on Snowflake or BigQuery. Decide placement by compliance, scale and cost. Use incremental models. Keep transformations versioned and tested. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Move and transform data to analytics COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Warehouse and lakehouse loading MAIN DRAWBACK Cost and compliance trade-offs ARCHITECTURAL KIND Data architecture

VI.11 Distributed Cache Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A cluster of cache nodes that holds frequently accessed data in memory across machines to cut latency and database load. Serve hot reads from fast, shared, partitioned memory instead of hitting the primary store. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Database bottlenecks and high latency for read-heavy workloads. Web scale made database round trips the dominant latency and cost. Cache-aside with a partitioned, replicated cache cluster Client Service / component Infrastructure Database / store Sync call How it works The application computes the key and finds its shard by consistent hashing. On a hit, the value returns from memory. On a miss, the app reads from the database. It writes the value to the cache with a TTL. Writes update the database and invalidate or update the cache. Replicas provide failover; nodes can be added with minimal key movement. DISTRIBUTED CACHE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Large reductions in latency and DB load. Stale data and invalidation complexity. + Horizontal scalability and high throughput. Cache stampede and hot keys. Shared state across application instances. Additional infrastructure to operate. Replication for availability. Cold-start and failover effects. When to use When not to use Read-heavy workloads, session storage, rate limiting and expensive computations. Write-heavy data needing strong consistency, or data sets with low reuse. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Redis caching product catalogs Session stores Set TTLs and eviction policies. Prevent stampedes with locking or request coalescing. Handle hot keys. Monitor hit ratio and memory. Leaderboards Rate-limiter counters. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Shared in-memory cache cluster COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Read-heavy workloads MAIN DRAWBACK Staleness and invalidation ARCHITECTURAL KIND Infrastructure pattern

VI.12 Hierarchical Caching Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Multiple cache levels — browser, CDN, application, distributed and database caches — each closer to different layers of the request path. Serve each request from the nearest cache that can answer it, falling through levels only on a miss. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Latency and load across a global request path where no single cache is sufficient. Different data has different scope and volatility; layered caches optimize cost, latency and hit ratio. Request falls through cache levels until a hit Client Infrastructure Database / store Sync call How it works The browser checks its local cache first. A miss goes to the CDN edge for static and cacheable responses. Next, the gateway or reverse proxy may return a cached response. The application checks an in-process cache, then a distributed cache. Only on a full miss does the database serve the request. Responses populate caches on the way back with appropriate TTLs. HIERARCHICAL CACHING ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Lowest latency for the most common requests. Multiple invalidation points and staleness risk. + Dramatically reduced origin and database load. Hard to reason about which layer served the data. Each tier absorbs different traffic patterns. Duplicated data across levels. Resilience when downstream is degraded. Complexity in coherence and testing. When to use When not to use High-traffic read-heavy systems with global users and mixed static and dynamic content. Highly personalized, rapidly changing data requiring strong freshness. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Global e-commerce product pages News sites Define per-layer TTLs and cache keys. Use versioned URLs for static assets and event-based invalidation for dynamic data. Measure hit ratio at every level. Streaming metadata. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Layered caches along the request path COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Global read-heavy systems MAIN DRAWBACK Invalidation across layers ARCHITECTURAL KIND Infrastructure pattern
