ARCHITECTURAL APPROACH VII.01 Cloud-Native Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Applications designed to exploit cloud elasticity: containerized, loosely coupled services managed by orchestration, automation and declarative infrastructure. Build for failure and change — immutable infrastructure, automation, observability and managed services as defaults. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Lift-and-shift apps that run in the cloud but do not use its elasticity, resilience or automation. The CNCF defined cloud-native around containers, microservices, dynamic orchestration and continuous delivery. Cloud-native building blocks working together Client Infrastructure Database / store Service / component Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works Code is built into immutable container images by CI. Images are deployed declaratively (GitOps) to an orchestrator. Ingress routes traffic to stateless services. Autoscalers adjust capacity to load. Services use managed databases, queues and storage. Observability and automated rollback keep the system healthy. CLOUD-NATIVE ARCHITECTURE ARCHITECTURAL APPROACH Advantages Disadvantages Elastic scalability and resilience. Steep learning curve and platform complexity. + Fast, automated and repeatable delivery. Distributed-system challenges. Efficient use of managed services. Cost management and sprawl. Portability across environments (containers). Skills and cultural change required. When to use When not to use Systems that need rapid delivery, elasticity and resilience on cloud infrastructure. Stable low-change workloads where traditional hosting is simpler and cheaper. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Large SaaS platforms Streaming services Design stateless services and externalize state. Use health probes, autoscaling and resource limits. Adopt IaC and GitOps. Build in observability from day one. Fintech platforms on Kubernetes. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Design applications for cloud elasticity COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium–High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Elastic, fast-delivery systems MAIN DRAWBACK Platform and skills complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural approach

VII.02 Kubernetes-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Applications run as Pods managed by Kubernetes, which schedules, scales, heals and networks containers across a cluster of nodes. Declare the desired state; controllers continuously reconcile reality to match it. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Manual placement, scaling and recovery of containers across many machines. Kubernetes became the standard container orchestrator for portable, self-healing deployments. Cluster with control plane, worker nodes, ingress and storage Client Infrastructure Database / store Service / component Sync call How it works Manifests (Deployments, Services, Ingress) are applied to the API server. State is stored in etcd; controllers reconcile desired vs actual. The scheduler places Pods onto nodes by resources and constraints. Services and ingress route traffic to healthy Pods. Probes restart failed Pods; autoscalers add replicas and nodes. Rolling updates replace Pods gradually and roll back on failure. KUBERNETES-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Self-healing, scaling and rolling updates. Operational and conceptual complexity. + Portable across clouds and on-premises. Overhead for small systems. Rich ecosystem (Helm, operators, service mesh). Networking and security configuration pitfalls. Declarative, automatable operations. Stateful workloads need care. When to use When not to use Many containerized services needing orchestration, autoscaling and portability. A few simple services or small teams where managed PaaS or serverless is easier. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Microservice platforms on EKS / GKE / AKS Internal developer platforms. Set resource requests and limits, probes and PodDisruptionBudgets. Spread across zones. Use namespaces and RBAC. Prefer managed control planes. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Orchestrated containers on a cluster COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Container fleets needing orchestration MAIN DRAWBACK Operational complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment topology

DEPLOYMENT APPROACH VII.03 Container-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Applications packaged with their dependencies into containers that run consistently on any host with a container runtime. Package once, run anywhere — isolated, lightweight and immutable runtime units. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED “Works on my machine” differences and heavy VMbased deployments. Docker made Linux containers easy to build, ship and run. Containers on a host from registry images Client Database / store Infrastructure Service / component Sync call How it works A Dockerfile defines the image with app and dependencies. CI builds and pushes the image to a registry. The runtime pulls the image on the host. It starts an isolated container using namespaces and cgroups. Networks and volumes connect containers to the world. Containers are replaced, not patched, for updates. CONTAINER-BASED ARCHITECTURE DEPLOYMENT APPROACH Advantages Disadvantages Consistent environments from laptop to production. Weaker isolation than VMs (shared kernel). + Lightweight and fast to start. Image and supply-chain security burden. High density versus VMs. Persistent data requires volumes. Strong CI/CD fit and immutability. Needs orchestration at scale. When to use When not to use Almost all modern deployments, microservices and CI environments. Workloads needing strong isolation or specialized hardware without careful setup. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Dockerized Spring Boot services CI build agents Use minimal base images and non-root users. Scan images. Keep containers stateless; use health checks. Pin image versions. Local dev environments with Docker Compose. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Packaged, isolated runtime units SCALABILITY High COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Shared-kernel isolation and supply chain COMPLEXITY Low–Medium MAINTAINABILITY High BEST USE CASE Portable consistent deployments ARCHITECTURAL Deployment approach KIND

EXECUTION MODEL VII.04 Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Code is deployed as individual stateless functions that run in response to events and are managed, scaled and billed per execution by the platform. The unit of deployment is a function; the platform handles runtime, scaling and isolation. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Provisioning and paying for servers for small, sporadic or event-driven units of work. AWS Lambda (2014) introduced fine-grained, payper-invocation compute. Triggers invoke ephemeral function instances External system Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works An event source triggers the function. If no warm instance exists, the platform cold-starts one. The function executes statelessly within time and memory limits. It reads and writes state in external services. The platform scales instances by concurrency. The instance is frozen or discarded after idle time; billing stops. FUNCTION-AS-A-SERVICE (FAAS) ARCHITECTURE EXECUTION MODEL Advantages Disadvantages No server management; per-invocation billing. Cold starts and execution time limits. + Automatic scaling, including to zero. Statelessness forces external state. Fast development for event handlers. Vendor-specific; complex local testing. Natural fit for glue logic. Cost grows at sustained high volume. When to use When not to use Event handlers, webhooks, scheduled tasks and bursty workloads. Long-running or latency-critical workloads, and steady high-throughput services. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Image thumbnails on upload Webhook processors Cron jobs Keep functions small and idempotent. Mitigate cold starts (provisioned concurrency, lightweight runtimes). Limit concurrency to protect downstream systems. Compare with Serverless in Part I. Data transformations. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Per-event stateless functions SCALABILITY Very high COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Cold starts and limits COMPLEXITY Low–Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Bursty event handlers ARCHITECTURAL Execution model KIND

VII.05 Event-Driven Serverless Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A serverless system in which managed event sources, buses and functions compose workflows without long-running servers. Chain managed services with events, so scaling and availability are properties of the platform. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Operating brokers and workers for event pipelines with spiky or unpredictable load. Cloud providers offered event buses, queues, workflows and functions that integrate natively. Managed event bus, queues and functions compose a workflow Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works A request or upload triggers an ingest function. The function stores data and emits an event to a bus. Rules route the event to queues, workflows or other functions. Queues buffer load and trigger processing functions in batches. Workflow services coordinate multi-step processes with retries. Dead-letter queues capture failures for inspection. EVENT-DRIVEN SERVERLESS ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Elastic and pay-per-use with minimal operations. Distributed debugging and tracing are harder. + Loose coupling between stages. Vendor lock-in with proprietary services. Built-in retries and integrations. At-least-once delivery requires idempotency. Fast to assemble. Cost can escalate at scale. When to use When not to use Spiky event pipelines, integration workflows, automation and backends with variable load. Steady high-throughput pipelines where containers are cheaper, or when portability is vital. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Order processing on AWS Image/video pipelines Define idempotency keys, DLQs and retry policies. Trace with correlation IDs. Cap concurrency. Track cost per event. IoT ingestion Notification systems. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Serverless services wired by events COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Variable-load event workflows MAIN DRAWBACK Lock-in and distributed debugging ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

VII.06 Multi-Cloud Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Using services from two or more cloud providers for the same system or portfolio. Avoid single-vendor dependence and exploit each provider’s strengths, at the cost of added complexity. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Vendor lock-in, regional gaps, compliance demands and provider-level outage risk. Enterprises acquire workloads across clouds or need negotiating leverage and resilience. A portable platform layer spanning two clouds Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works A global traffic manager routes requests among clouds. Workloads are packaged in containers for portability. Infrastructure is defined with provider-neutral IaC. Identity, observability and CI/CD are cloud-agnostic. Data replication or partitioning handles state across clouds. Failover shifts traffic if a provider or region fails. MULTI-CLOUD ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Reduced lock-in and negotiating leverage. Significant complexity, cost and skills demands. + Resilience to provider-wide outages. Lowest-common-denominator services reduce + Access to best-of-breed services and regional benefits. presence. Cross-cloud data transfer cost and latency. + Supports regulatory constraints. Security and governance fragmentation. When to use When not to use Regulated or very large organizations with real requirements for provider diversity. Most systems; the complexity usually outweighs the benefits — multi-region on one cloud is often sufficient. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Banks with regulator-mandated exit plans Global SaaS with customer-chosen clouds. Standardize on Kubernetes, Terraform and open telemetry. Minimize cross-cloud data flows. Decide which services are portable and which are deliberately provider-specific. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Workloads across multiple cloud providers COMPLEXITY Very high SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Low–Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Regulated or lock-in-sensitive systems MAIN DRAWBACK Complexity and cost ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment topology

VII.07 Hybrid Cloud Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Combines on-premises or private infrastructure with public cloud, integrated to operate as a single environment. Keep sensitive or legacy workloads on-premises while using the cloud for elasticity and new services. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Data residency, latency, legacy dependencies and capital investment while still gaining cloud benefits. Few enterprises can move everything at once; regulations and legacy systems keep some workloads on-premises. On-premises datacenter connected securely to public cloud Service / component Database / store Infrastructure Client Sync call How it works Users reach cloud front ends or on-premises systems through consistent identity. A private connection links the datacenter to the cloud network. Sensitive data and legacy systems stay on-premises. Cloud applications call on-premises systems through secured APIs. Burst workloads scale out into the cloud. Unified monitoring and policy cover both environments. V I I .07 HYBRID CLOUD ARCHITECTURE Advantages Meets data residency and compliance needs. + Gradual migration and use of existing investments. Cloud elasticity for burst demand. Lower latency for on-premises dependencies. When to use Regulated enterprises, phased migrations and workloads tied to on-premises data or hardware. Real-world applications Banks keeping core ledgers on-premises Hospitals with local data Manufacturing with edge plants. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE On-premises integrated with public cloud SCALABILITY High COUPLING Medium MAIN DRAWBACK Dual-environment complexity Disadvantages Operational complexity across two environments. Network latency and bandwidth between sites. Duplicate tooling and skills. Consistent security and governance are hard. When not to use Greenfield startups without on-premises constraints. Key engineering considerations Size and secure the link. Use consistent tooling (Kubernetes, IaC) on both sides. Keep chatty calls inside one environment. Plan identity and observability across sites. COMPLEXITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Regulated and legacy-heavy enterprises ARCHITECTURAL Deployment topology KIND

VII.08 Edge Computing Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Processing is moved close to data sources and users on devices, gateways or edge nodes — rather than in a distant central cloud. Compute where data is created to reduce latency, bandwidth cost and dependence on connectivity. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Latency, bandwidth, privacy and offline needs for IoT, video and real-time applications. Billions of devices generate data that is costly or too slow to ship to central data centers. Devices, edge nodes and cloud in a hierarchy Client Service / component Database / store Infrastructure Sync call Async / event How it works Devices send raw data to a nearby edge gateway. The gateway filters and aggregates data and runs local inference. Time-critical decisions return to devices without a cloud round trip. Summaries and exceptions are forwarded to regional and cloud tiers. The cloud trains models and manages fleets. Updated models and configuration are pushed back to the edge. EDGE COMPUTING ARCHITECTURE Advantages Very low latency and local autonomy. + Reduced bandwidth and cloud costs. Works through intermittent connectivity. Keeps sensitive data local. When to use IoT, industrial automation, video analytics, AR/VR and latency-sensitive services. Real-world applications Factory predictive maintenance Retail video analytics Connected vehicles CDN edge functions. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Compute near data sources SCALABILITY Very high COUPLING Low MAIN DRAWBACK Fleet management and constrained resources Disadvantages Distributed fleet management and updates are hard. Limited compute and storage at the edge. Security surface across many devices. Data consistency between tiers. When not to use Workloads without latency, bandwidth or privacy needs where central cloud suffices. Key engineering considerations Design for offline-first and store-and-forward. Automate secure OTA updates. Define what runs at each tier. Monitor device health centrally. COMPLEXITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium BEST USE CASE Latency-critical, bandwidth-heavy IoT ARCHITECTURAL Deployment topology KIND

VII.09 CDN-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Static and cacheable content is served from globally distributed edge servers, shielding the origin and reducing latency. Bring content geographically close to users and absorb traffic at the edge. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Latency for global users and origin overload from repeated requests. Web traffic is dominated by cacheable assets and media; CDNs made global delivery affordable. Users served from edge caches; origin only on miss Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call How it works DNS directs the user to the nearest edge PoP. The edge serves cached content on a hit. On a miss, it asks an origin shield, which may also hold the object. Only a shield miss reaches the origin. The response is cached according to Cache-Control headers. Purge or versioned URLs refresh updated content. CDN-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Low latency and high availability for global users. Cache invalidation and stale content. + Huge origin offload and cost savings. Limited use for highly dynamic personalized + DDoS and WAF protection at the edge. content. + Handles traffic spikes. Extra vendor dependency and cost. Debugging across edge and origin. When to use When not to use Websites, media streaming, software downloads and APIs with cacheable responses. Fully dynamic, uncacheable, per-user content with no static components. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Netflix Open Connect Cloudflare / CloudFront / Akamai fronted sites Use immutable, versioned assets with long TTLs. Define cache keys and vary headers carefully. Enable origin shield and compression. Monitor hit ratio. Software update distribution. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Serve content from global edge caches COMPLEXITY Low–Medium SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Global static and media delivery MAIN DRAWBACK Invalidation and dynamic content limits ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment topology

VII.10 High Availability Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Eliminating single points of failure through redundancy and automatic failover so the system meets an availability target (for example 99.99%). Replicate every critical component across failure domains and detect and route around failures automatically. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Downtime caused by component, host or zone failures. Business-critical services have strict uptime SLAs and revenue impact per minute of outage. Redundancy across availability zones Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Traffic enters through redundant, health-checked load balancers. Stateless instances run in at least two or three availability zones. Data stores are replicated with automatic failover. Health checks remove failed instances from rotation. A standby is promoted when the primary fails. Capacity headroom ensures survivors can carry the load. HIGH AVAILABILITY ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages High uptime and resilience to zone and host failures. Higher infrastructure and operational cost. + Planned maintenance without downtime. Added complexity in replication and failover. Predictable failover behavior. + Improved customer trust. Cannot protect against logical errors and bad deployments. Needs regular failover testing. When to use When not to use Customer-facing and revenue-critical systems with strict uptime targets. Internal or batch systems where brief downtime is acceptable. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Payment gateways E-commerce checkout Define SLOs and error budgets. Remove every single point of failure, including DNS and secrets. Test failover with game days. Keep headroom for N+1. Core banking channels. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Redundancy and automatic failover COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Uptime-critical systems MAIN DRAWBACK Cost and failover complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Quality-attribute architecture

VII.11 Fault-Tolerant Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A design that continues operating correctly in the presence of component failures, using redundancy, isolation and graceful degradation. Assume failures will occur; contain them and keep serving, possibly with reduced functionality. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Cascading failures and total outages when a dependency or component misbehaves. Distributed systems have constant partial failure; resilience must be designed in (Release It!, chaos engineering). Resilience patterns around a service call Client Service / component Infrastructure External system Sync call How it works Requests pass a rate limiter that protects capacity. Calls use bulkheads so one dependency cannot exhaust shared resources. Timeouts bound waiting time. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter handle transient errors. The circuit breaker opens after repeated failures and fails fast. A fallback provides degraded but useful results. FAULT-TOLERANT ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Prevents cascading failures. Added configuration and testing complexity. + Graceful degradation keeps core flows alive. Wrong thresholds cause false trips or retry storms. Faster recovery and bounded resource use. Fallbacks may serve stale or incorrect data. Proven, well-known patterns. Needs observability to tune. When to use When not to use Any distributed system with remote dependencies, especially microservices. Not applicable as a whole; apply patterns selectively to avoid overengineering. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Resilience4j in Spring services Netflix Hystrix-style protection Set timeouts everywhere. Retry only idempotent calls with jitter. Size bulkheads from capacity data. Test with chaos experiments and load tests. Payment gateway integrations. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Contain failures and degrade gracefully COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY High MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Systems with many remote dependencies MAIN DRAWBACK Threshold tuning and retry storms ARCHITECTURAL KIND Quality-attribute architecture

VII.12 Disaster Recovery Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Planned capability to restore systems and data after a major outage, defined by RPO (data loss tolerance) and RTO (recovery time). Choose a recovery strategy matching business tolerance, from backup and restore to warm standby and multi-site active-active. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Loss of an entire site or region, data corruption and ransomware. Regulations and business continuity plans require tested recovery objectives. DR strategies from cheap and slow to costly and fast Service / component Database / store Infrastructure Sync call Async / event How it works Define RPO and RTO per system and data class. Replicate data or take snapshots to another region. Keep the DR stack as backup-restore, pilot light, warm standby or hot. Detect the disaster and decide to declare it. Automation recreates or scales up the DR stack and promotes data. Traffic is switched and later failed back after repair. DISASTER RECOVERY ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Business continuity with defined recovery targets. Ongoing cost for replicas and standby capacity. + Protection from regional failure, corruption and DR plans rot unless exercised. ransomware (immutable backups). Data loss possible according to RPO. + Cost can scale with required RTO/RPO. Failback is complex. + Meets regulatory expectations. When to use When not to use All business-critical systems, scaled to their RTO/RPO. Throwaway environments; do not over-invest in DR for non-critical systems. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Banks with DR sites Healthcare record systems Write runbooks and automate with IaC. Test regularly (game days). Keep backups immutable and verify restores. Monitor replication lag against RPO. Cloud multi-region DR for ERP. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Recover from site or region loss COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Business continuity requirements MAIN DRAWBACK Cost and plan decay ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment topology

VII.13 Auto-Scaling Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Capacity adjusts automatically to demand by adding or removing instances, based on metrics, schedules or predictions. Match resources to load continuously so the system is neither overloaded nor wasteful. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Manual capacity management and the cost of provisioning for peak load all the time. Cloud elasticity allows rapid provisioning and persecond billing. A feedback loop from metrics to scaling decisions Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works Metrics (CPU, requests, latency, queue depth) are collected. The autoscaler compares them with target thresholds. It adds capacity when load rises and removes it when it falls. New instances register with the load balancer after health checks. Cooldowns prevent flapping. Scheduled or predictive rules prepare for known peaks. AUTO-SCALING ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Cost efficiency and resilience to load spikes. + Hands-off capacity management. Scaling lag and cold starts; poorly tuned policies cause flapping. + Improved availability under load. Stateful services scale poorly. + Supports event-driven scaling (queue length). Downstream systems may become the bottleneck. Cost can spike unexpectedly. When to use When not to use Variable or unpredictable workloads on cloud or Kubernetes. Fixed steady workloads or stateful systems without scalable design. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Kubernetes HPA and KEDA AWS Auto Scaling groups Retail events and flash sales. Keep services stateless. Scale on leading indicators such as queue depth. Set min/max bounds, warm-up and cooldown. Load-test scaling behavior and protect databases. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Dynamic capacity by demand COMPLEXITY Medium SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Variable-load workloads MAIN DRAWBACK Scaling lag and downstream bottlenecks ARCHITECTURAL KIND Deployment pattern

VIII.01 Rule-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Behavior is expressed as declarative business rules evaluated by a rule engine against facts, rather than hard-coded in procedural logic. Separate the frequently changing “what to do when” from the stable application code so rules can change without redeployment. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Complex, volatile decision logic scattered across code that business users cannot review or change. Expert systems and business rule management systems (Drools, ILOG) made rules first-class artifacts. Rule engine matches facts against a rule base Client Domain core Database / store External system Sync call How it works The application inserts facts into working memory. The engine matches facts against rule conditions. Matching rules form a conflict set. Conflict resolution chooses which rule fires. Actions update facts or trigger side effects, possibly firing further rules. The final decisions are returned to the application. RULE-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Business-readable, changeable rules without redeployment. Hard to debug rule interactions and ordering. Rule bases can become unmanageable. + Separation of volatile logic from code. Performance depends on rule design. + Consistent, auditable decisions. Extra tooling and skills. + Efficient matching (Rete) for many rules. When to use When not to use Pricing, eligibility, fraud scoring, compliance and underwriting decisions that change often. Simple logic that a few conditionals handle; stable workflows. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Insurance underwriting Loan eligibility engines Version and test rule sets like code. Limit rule chaining depth. Log fired rules for audit. Consider decision tables (DMN) for readability. Promotion and pricing rules Fraud detection. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Declarative rules evaluated by an engine COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Volatile business decision logic MAIN DRAWBACK Rule interaction and tooling complexity ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

VIII.02 Interpreter Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A system interprets a program or script in a domain language at runtime by parsing it and executing its structure with an engine. Embed a language (DSL) so behavior is expressed as data that the interpreter evaluates. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Needing flexible, user-defined or frequently changing behavior without rebuilding the application. Scripting, query languages and workflow engines require runtime evaluation of external definitions. Client Service / component Database / store External system Sync call How it works The user or system supplies a script or expression. The lexer and parser build an abstract syntax tree. The evaluator walks the tree node by node. Variables and functions are resolved in the runtime context. Results and side effects are produced. Errors are reported with source positions. INTERPRETER ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Behavior changes without recompiling or redeploying. Slower than compiled code. Security risks of executing untrusted scripts. + Enables user-defined logic and extensibility. Debugging and tooling for the DSL are costly. + Isolates domain concepts in a DSL. Language design is hard. + Natural for expression and query evaluation. When to use When not to use Rule expressions, query languages, templating, workflow definitions and configuration with logic. Hot paths needing maximum performance or untrusted input without sandboxing. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spring Expression Language (SpEL) SQL engines Sandbox execution with timeouts and resource limits. Validate and type-check before evaluation. Cache parsed ASTs. Keep the language small. Workflow engines (BPMN) Template engines. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Execute external DSL scripts at runtime COMPLEXITY Medium–High SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Runtime-configurable behavior MAIN DRAWBACK Performance and security risk ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

VIII.03 Reflection-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A system with a base level (application logic) and a meta level that inspects and modifies the system’s structure and behavior at runtime. Expose the system’s own types, configuration and behavior to be examined and changed dynamically. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Rigid applications that cannot adapt to new types, configurations or extensions without recompilation. Frameworks needed to discover and wire components dynamically (dependency injection, serialization, ORMs). Base level behavior is controlled through a meta level Domain core Service / component Infrastructure Sync call How it works The framework scans classes and reads metadata (annotations, types). Metaobjects describe structure and behavior. The framework instantiates and wires objects via the reflection API. It invokes methods or maps fields dynamically. Changes to the meta level alter base-level behavior. Proxies and interceptors apply cross-cutting behavior. REFLECTION-BASED ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages High flexibility and extensibility. Slower than static calls and harder to optimize. + Powers frameworks with convention over Weaker compile-time safety and harder debugging. configuration. Obscure failures at runtime. + Reduces boilerplate (DI, serialization, ORM). Breaks with native-image and obfuscation unless + Supports plug-ins and dynamic loading. configured. When to use When not to use Frameworks and infrastructure: DI containers, ORMs, serializers, test tools and plug-in systems. Business logic where explicit code is clearer and safer. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spring DI and annotations Hibernate Jackson Confine reflection to infrastructure. Cache lookups. For GraalVM native images, register reflective access ahead of time. Prefer compile-time processing where possible. JUnit. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Runtime self-inspection and modification COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Low–Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Frameworks and extensible platforms MAIN DRAWBACK Opaque runtime failures and overhead ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

REPLICATION TOPOLOGY VIII.04 Master–Slave / Primary–Replica Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA One primary node handles writes and propagates changes to replica nodes, which typically serve reads and act as failover standbys. A single writer simplifies consistency; replicas scale reads and provide redundancy. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Read scaling and availability for databases and services with a clear single source of truth. Simple, predictable replication underlies MySQL, PostgreSQL and Redis setups (the term “primary– replica” replaces “master–slave”). Writes to the primary; replicas serve reads and standby Client Infrastructure Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works The application sends writes to the primary. The primary commits and records changes in a replication log. Replicas apply the log asynchronously or synchronously. Reads are routed to replicas to reduce primary load. If the primary fails, a replica is promoted. Replication lag can make replica reads stale. MASTER–SLAVE / PRIMARY–REPLICA ARCHITECTURE REPLICATION TOPOLOGY Advantages Disadvantages Simple consistency model with one writer. Write throughput is limited to one node. + Read scalability and redundancy. Replication lag causes stale reads. Replicas support backups and analytics without affecting the primary. Failover can lose recent writes (async) or add latency (sync). + Well-supported in most databases. Promotion and split-brain risks. When to use When not to use Read-heavy workloads and databases needing simple, strongly ordered writes. Write-heavy or multi-region active-active write needs (consider sharding or multi-primary). Real-world applications Key engineering considerations MySQL/PostgreSQL replication Redis primary-replica Reporting replicas. Route read-your-writes traffic to the primary. Monitor lag. Use automated failover with fencing to avoid splitbrain. Plan for sharding when writes outgrow one node. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Single writer, replicated readers COMPLEXITY Low–Medium SCALABILITY Medium — read scaling only MAINTAINABILITY High COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Read-heavy databases MAIN DRAWBACK Single write node and replica lag ARCHITECTURAL KIND Replication topology

COORDINATION PATTERN VIII.05 Leader–Follower Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA A cluster elects one leader to coordinate decisions or serialize writes; followers replicate the leader’s state and take over if it fails. Use consensus-based election so the group always agrees on a single leader, even across failures. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Coordination, ordering and automatic failover in distributed clusters without manual promotion. Consensus algorithms (Paxos, Raft) made leader election safe and standard in systems like etcd, Kafka and ZooKeeper. Raft-style leader replicates a log to followers by quorum Client Domain core Service / component Database / store Sync call Async / event How it works Nodes elect a leader through a majority vote. Clients send writes to the leader. The leader appends entries and replicates them to followers. An entry commits once a quorum acknowledges it. Heartbeats prove the leader is alive. If the leader fails, followers time out and elect a new leader. LEADER–FOLLOWER ARCHITECTURE COORDINATION PATTERN Advantages Disadvantages Automatic, safe failover with strong consistency. Leader is a throughput bottleneck. + Clear ordering of operations. Elections cause brief unavailability. Proven consensus algorithms. + Tolerates minority node failures. Needs an odd number of nodes and low-latency links. Cross-region quorum raises write latency. When to use When not to use Coordination services, metadata stores, strongly consistent replicated state and cluster management. Very high write throughput or multi-region low-latency writes without partitioning. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations etcd and Kubernetes control plane Kafka KRaft controllers ZooKeeper Run 3 or 5 nodes across failure domains. Tune election timeouts. Keep leader workloads light. Distinguish from primary–replica: leader–follower adds consensus and automatic election. Consul. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Elected leader with quorum replication COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Medium MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Medium BEST USE CASE Strongly consistent coordination MAIN DRAWBACK Leader bottleneck and quorum latency ARCHITECTURAL KIND Coordination pattern

VIII.06 Reactive Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Systems that are responsive, resilient, elastic and message-driven, as defined by the Reactive Manifesto, often using non-blocking I/O and backpressure. Build on asynchronous, non-blocking message passing so components stay responsive under load and failure. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Thread-per-request blocking that wastes resources and limits scalability under high concurrency. High concurrency and latency-sensitive systems needed efficient resource use and graceful degradation. Non-blocking pipeline with backpressure Client Infrastructure Service / component External system Database / store Queue / broker Sync call Async / event How it works A small pool of event-loop threads accepts many connections. Handlers build a reactive pipeline instead of blocking. I/O calls return immediately with a publisher. Subscribers request N items, applying backpressure to producers. Results flow as signals when data is available. Errors and timeouts propagate as events with fallbacks. REACTIVE ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages High concurrency with few threads. Steep learning curve and hard debugging. + Efficient resource use and low latency under load. Entire stack must be non-blocking; blocking calls + Backpressure prevents overload. ruin benefits. + Composable asynchronous flows. Complex stack traces and testing. Virtual threads (Java 21+) can offer simpler alternatives. When to use When not to use Streaming, high-concurrency gateways, I/O-bound services and real-time systems. CPU-bound or simple CRUD services where blocking code on virtual threads is simpler. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Spring WebFlux services API gateways on Netty Never block event-loop threads. Use bounded buffers and timeouts. Measure before adopting: compare with virtual threads. Use reactive drivers end to end. Reactive Kafka pipelines Trading price streams. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Non-blocking, message-driven responsiveness COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE High -concurrency I/O-bound services MAIN DRAWBACK Complexity and debugging difficulty ARCHITECTURAL KIND Architectural style

CONCURRENCY ARCHITECTURE VIII.07 Actor-Based Architecture WHAT IS IT? FUNDAMENTAL IDEA Computation is organized as independent actors that own private state and communicate only by asynchronous messages. Share nothing, send messages: each actor processes one message at a time, eliminating locks. PROBLEM IT SOLVES WHY IT WAS INTRODUCED Shared-memory concurrency bugs and difficulty scaling and distributing stateful logic. Hewitt’s Actor model, realized in Erlang and Akka, enabled massively concurrent and fault-tolerant systems. Actors with mailboxes under a supervision hierarchy Domain core Service / component External system Sync call Async / event How it works Each actor has private state and a mailbox. Actors send immutable messages asynchronously. An actor processes one message at a time, so no locks are needed. An actor can create child actors and change its behavior. Supervisors restart failed children (“let it crash”). Actors can be located on remote nodes transparently. ACTOR-BASED ARCHITECTURE CONCURRENCY ARCHITECTURE Advantages Disadvantages Simple concurrency without locks. + Natural fault isolation and supervision. Message-passing complexity and harder debugging. + Scales across cores and machines. Mailbox overload and backpressure need design. + Good fit for stateful, entity-oriented workloads. Eventual consistency between actors. Unfamiliar model for many teams. When to use When not to use Stateful entities at scale (devices, sessions, games), telecom, trading and highly concurrent systems. Simple stateless CRUD services and CPU-bound batch work. Real-world applications Key engineering considerations Erlang telecom switches Akka-based IoT platforms Orleans (virtual actors) for gaming Keep messages immutable and small. Bound mailboxes and apply backpressure. Design supervision strategies. Persist actor state with event sourcing when needed. Akka Cluster Sharding. Quick summary PRIMARY PURPOSE Isolated actors communicating by messages COMPLEXITY High SCALABILITY Very high MAINTAINABILITY Medium COUPLING Low BEST USE CASE Stateful, highly concurrent entities MAIN DRAWBACK Debugging and unfamiliar programming model ARCHITECTURAL KIND Concurrency architecture

IX.01 Monolith vs Modular Monolith vs Microservices The three differ in two independent decisions: how strongly code is partitioned (logical boundaries) and how it is deployed (one unit or many). A modular monolith keeps the second constant while fixing the first. Monolith Modular monolith Microservices Client Module Database / store Domain core Infrastructure Service / component Sync call Async / event Dependency direction Fundamental differences ASPECT MONOLITH MODULAR MONOLITH MICROSERVICES Deployment unit One One Many Boundaries Convention only Enforced modules Network contracts Data One shared schema Schema per module Database per service Transactions Local ACID Local ACID Sagas / eventual Team scaling Poor Good Very good Ops overhead Lowest Low Highest Failure isolation None Weak Strong MONOLITH VS MODULAR MONOLITH VS MICROSERVICES Advantages & disadvantages OPTION ADVANTAGES DISADVANTAGES Monolith Simplest to build, test and run; lowest latency Coupling decays structure; single scale and release unit Modular Boundaries without distribution cost; easy refactoring; Discipline needed; still one deploy/scale unit monolith path to extraction Microservices Independent deploy and scale; fault isolation; team autonomy Distributed complexity, eventual consistency, heavy operations Complexity trade-offs Suitable use cases Complexity moves from code (monolith) to boundaries (modular) to infrastructure and data (microservices). The other three buy independence from frameworks and databases at the cost of interfaces, mapping and discipline. Their structural differences are small: they enforce the same inward dependency rule with different vocabulary. Layered: CRUD-heavy apps with simple rules. Clean: long-lived apps with explicit use cases and several delivery channels. Hexagonal: integration-heavy services with many adapters. Onion: DDD-driven domains with rich models. Practical recommendation. Use layered for simple CRUD. For non-trivial domains pick the hexagonal vocabulary (ports/adapters) with DDD tactical patterns inside; treat Clean and Onion as equivalent variations rather than competing choices. Enforce the dependency rule with ArchUnit.

SOA optimizes enterprise-wide reuse and integration through shared middleware; microservices optimize independent delivery with smart endpoints and dumb pipes. SOA Microservices Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Queue / broker Sync call Async / event Fundamental differences ASPECT SOA MICROSERVICES Service granularity Coarse, business-process Fine, bounded context Integration Central ESB, orchestration Smart endpoints, simple HTTP/events Data Often shared databases Database per service Governance Centralized, standardized Decentralized, team-owned Protocols SOAP/XML, WS-* REST, gRPC, messaging Deployment Often shared runtime Independent containers Primary goal Reuse and integration Autonomy and speed SOA VS MICROSERVICES Advantages & disadvantages OPTION ADVANTAGES DISADVANTAGES SOA Integrates legacy; central governance and security; reuse ESB bottleneck; slow change; heavy contracts Microservices Independent deployment and scaling; tech freedom Operational complexity; distributed data Complexity trade-offs Suitable use cases SOA centralizes complexity in the bus and governance; microservices distribute it across services and infrastructure. IX.04 MVC vs MVP vs MVVM vs MVI All separate presentation from data. They differ in who owns presentation logic and how state flows to the view: controller-driven, presenter-driven, binding-driven or unidirectional reducerdriven. IX.05 Event-Driven vs Message-Driven Both are asynchronous. In event-driven systems producers announce facts and do not care who reacts; in message-driven systems a sender addresses a message to a recipient expecting it to be handled. Event-driven — facts, many unknown subscribers Message-driven — command to one handler Service / component Queue / broker Sync call Async / event Fundamental differences ASPECT EVENT-DRIVEN MESSAGE-DRIVEN Message intent Notification of a fact (past tense) Command or request (imperative) Addressing Topic; producer unaware of consumers Queue/endpoint; sender knows recipient role Consumers Many independent One (competing) handler Coupling Lowest Low Flow control Consumers decide Sender expects action Example OrderPlaced ProcessPayment EVENT-DRIVEN VS MESSAGE-DRIVEN Advantages & disadvantages OPTION ADVANTAGES DISADVANTAGES Event-driven Extensible fan-out; producers stay unchanged Hard to trace flow; eventual consistency Message-driven Reliable work distribution; clear responsibility Sender coupled to the existence of a handler Complexity trade-offs Suitable use cases Events reduce coupling most but hide control flow; messages keep a clearer chain of responsibility but couple sender to a capability. Most systems combine both: commands inside a service boundary, events between boundaries. Event-driven: broadcasting state changes to unknown or growing consumers. Message-driven: delegating work that must be done exactly by one worker. Practical recommendation. Use events to publish facts across service boundaries and commands via queues for work that must be performed. Name messages accordingly (OrderPlaced vs ProcessPayment) to keep intent clear.

CQRS separates the models for writing and reading; Event Sourcing changes how state is stored — as an append-only event log. IX.07 Orchestration vs Choreography Both coordinate multi-service processes. Orchestration puts the process logic in one controller; choreography distributes it across services reacting to events. IX.08 Serverless vs Container-Based Architecture Both avoid managing physical servers. Serverless abstracts runtime and scaling entirely and bills per execution; containers give you control over the runtime and typically bill for provisioned capacity. IX.09 Microkernel vs Plugin-Based Architecture Both keep a small core and put variable behavior outside it. A microkernel is a minimal runtime that routes between modules as the system’s essential structure; a plug-in architecture is a complete application with extension points for optional add-ons. Banking and payments HLD Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker Database / store External system Sync call Async / event MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Accounts, Payments orchestrator, Ledger, Fraud, AML/compliance, Limits, Notifications, Reconciliation, Identity. Synchronous calls for authorization and fraud scoring; Kafka for payment events, audit and reconciliation; idempotency keys on every payment request. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES Double-entry ledger as append-only events (event sourcing); relational store for accounts; WORM archive for audit; warehouse for analytics. Payment networks (UPI, card, SWIFT), core banking, KYC providers, credit bureaus, HSM/KMS. CHOSEN ARCHITECTURAL STYLE WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE WAS SELECTED Event-sourced ledger with orchestrated sagas, hexagonal services and active-passive multi-region DR. The ledger must be auditable and never lose or doublepost a transaction, so immutable events and idempotent commands are preferred. Orchestration gives payments a visible, regulated state machine. KEY TRADE-OFFS Higher engineering and operational cost; strong consistency limits throughput per account; active-passive DR accepts minutes of RTO for simpler data correctness.

X.03 Food Delivery Platform A three-sided marketplace (customers, restaurants, couriers) with real-time location and dispatch. It shows geo-indexed matching, event-driven state and push-based tracking. Food delivery HLD Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker Database / store External system Sync call Async / event MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Order, Restaurant/Menu, Dispatch, ETA and pricing, Tracking, Payment, Notification, Rating. REST for ordering; Kafka for order state events; WebSocket/SSE push for live tracking; high-frequency GPS via a streaming ingestion path. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES PostgreSQL for orders; Redis GEO or specialized geospatial store for courier locations; Elasticsearch for restaurant search; object storage for images. Maps/routing, payment provider, SMS/push providers, restaurant POS integrations. CHOSEN ARCHITECTURAL STYLE WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE WAS SELECTED Event-driven microservices with a real-time streaming edge and geospatial indexing. Dispatch quality depends on fresh location data and fast matching, so location state lives in memoryoptimized geo stores and state changes flow as events. Order data stays transactional. KEY TRADE-OFFS Eventual consistency in tracking and ETA; location firehose cost; dispatch algorithm complexity; surge handling at meal peaks needs autoscaling and queues.

X.04 Video Streaming Platform A read-dominated, bandwidth-heavy system where the data path (video bytes) is separated from the control path (metadata, playback, recommendations). Video streaming HLD Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker Database / store External system Sync call Async / event MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Catalog, Playback/DRM, Search, Recommendation, User/Subscription, Upload, Transcoding, Analytics. REST/GraphQL for control plane; HTTP adaptive streaming (HLS/DASH) via CDN for video; queues for transcoding jobs; Kafka for viewing events. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES Object storage for master files and renditions; relational/NoSQL for metadata; feature store for recommendations; data lake for analytics. CDN/ISP caches, DRM license servers, payment providers, device vendors. CHOSEN ARCHITECTURAL STYLE WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE WAS SELECTED Microservices control plane with a CDN-based data plane, a fan-out/fan-in transcoding pipeline and stream processing for telemetry. Video bytes dominate cost and latency, so they bypass application services and are delivered from edge caches. Transcoding is embarrassingly parallel, so it uses queues and elastic workers. KEY TRADE-OFFS CDN cost and cache-fill complexity; transcoding compute cost; recommendation freshness vs cost; DRM adds device-specific complexity.

X.05 Ride Booking Platform A real-time marketplace where supply (drivers) and demand (riders) are matched within seconds. It highlights location streaming, geo-sharding and eventually consistent state with idempotent trip lifecycle. Ride booking HLD Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker Database / store External system Sync call Async / event MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Rider and driver apps, Trip, Matching, Location, Pricing/surge, Payments, ETA, Notifications, Fraud. Persistent WebSocket for driver location and offers; Kafka for trip events; synchronous calls for pricing and ETA; idempotent trip state transitions. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES In-memory geo index sharded by cell; relational store for trips; time-series store for location history; data lake for analytics and ML. Maps/routing, payment processors, SMS/push, identity verification. CHOSEN ARCHITECTURAL STYLE WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE WAS SELECTED Event-driven microservices with geo-sharded inmemory state and a streaming location pipeline. Matching needs sub-second access to current driver positions, so hot location state is partitioned geographically in memory. Trip lifecycle is a state machine published as events so pricing, payments and notifications react independently. KEY TRADE-OFFS Geographic sharding complicates cross-region trips; dispatch-quality tuning; surge pricing fairness; heavy location traffic cost.

X.06 Social Media Platform A write-light, read-heavy system with graph relationships and a personalized feed. It shows the fan-out choice (write vs read) and layered caching. Social media HLD Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker Database / store Sync call Async / event MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Post, Feed/Timeline, Social graph, Media, Search, Notification, Moderation, Ads. REST/GraphQL APIs; Kafka for post events; async fanout workers; push notifications; CDN for media. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES Sharded relational or wide-column store for posts; graph or adjacency store for relationships; Redis for timeline caches; object storage for media; search index. Push providers (APNs/FCM), CDN, ML moderation services, ad platforms. CHOSEN ARCHITECTURAL STYLE WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE WAS SELECTED Event-driven microservices with CQRS-style read models (timelines), hierarchical caching and CDNbased media delivery. Reads vastly outnumber writes, so timelines are precomputed (fan-out on write) for normal users and merged at read time for celebrities. Events decouple posting from feed building, search indexing and notifications. KEY TRADE-OFFS Fan-out storage cost and delay; hot-key celebrity accounts; eventual consistency of feeds; moderation and ranking complexity.

X.07 Notification Platform A shared internal platform that delivers email, SMS, push and in-app messages reliably at scale. It illustrates queue-based load leveling, per-channel isolation and idempotent delivery. Notification platform HLD Client Infrastructure Service / component Queue / broker External system Database / store Sync call Async / event MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Notification API, Template service, User preference service, Router and rate limiter, Channel workers, Delivery tracker, Provider adapters. Producers send requests via API or Kafka; per-channel queues decouple speeds; workers call provider APIs; delivery receipts return via webhooks. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES Request log in Kafka; status and deduplication store (Redis/DynamoDB); template store; preference database; analytics store. Email (SES/SendGrid), SMS gateways, APNs/FCM, WhatsApp APIs. CHOSEN ARCHITECTURAL STYLE WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE WAS SELECTED Message-driven architecture with competing consumers, ports-and-adapters provider integrations and per-channel bulkheads. Providers are slow, rate-limited and flaky, so queues absorb bursts and isolate channels. Adapters make providers replaceable; idempotency keys prevent duplicate sends. KEY TRADE-OFFS At-least-once delivery requires dedupe; ordering is weak; provider failover logic; compliance with user preferences and quiet hours adds complexity.

X.08 Large-Scale Data Processing Platform A platform ingesting billions of events per day for both real-time and historical analytics. It shows how Kappa-style streaming, lakehouse storage and medallion layers compose. Data processing platform HLD External system Queue / broker Service / component Database / store Infrastructure Client Sync call Async / event Dependency direction MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Ingestion (Kafka Connect, CDC), Stream processors, Batch processing, Orchestrator, Catalog and lineage, Serving stores, Feature store. Kafka as the central log; stream processors consume and produce topics; batch jobs read and write lakehouse tables; orchestrator schedules and monitors. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES Object storage with Delta/Iceberg tables in Bronze/Silver/Gold layers; low-latency OLAP store for real-time dashboards; feature store; metadata catalog. Source databases and SaaS exports, BI tools, ML platforms, identity and secrets management. CHOSEN ARCHITECTURAL STYLE WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE WAS SELECTED Kappa-style streaming with a lakehouse and medallion layering, plus orchestrated batch for heavy backfills. A replayable log lets both real-time and historical use cases share one pipeline; the lakehouse gives ACID tables and governance on cheap storage; medallion layers make quality explicit. KEY TRADE-OFFS Operational complexity of streaming and state; storage and compute cost; schema evolution and backfill coordination; skills requirement.

X.09 Enterprise SaaS Platform A multi-tenant B2B product serving thousands of organizations with different sizes and compliance needs. It illustrates tenancy models, cell-based isolation and tenant-aware observability. Enterprise SaaS HLD Client Infrastructure Service / component Database / store Queue / broker External system Sync call Async / event MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Gateway and tenant router, Identity/SSO, Core product services, Integration and webhook service, Metering and billing, Admin/provisioning, Audit logging. REST APIs and webhooks for integrations; events for metering and audit; tenant context propagated in tokens and headers. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES Pooled database with row-level security for small tenants; schema- or database-per-tenant for larger ones; per-tenant encryption keys; object storage with tenant prefixes; audit log store. X.10 IoT Device Management Platform A platform connecting millions of devices that send telemetry and receive commands and firmware updates, often over unreliable links. It shows edge processing, MQTT ingestion and device twins. IoT device management HLD Client Service / component Infrastructure Queue / broker Database / store External system Sync call Async / event MAJOR SERVICES & COMPONENTS COMMUNICATION MECHANISMS Device registry and provisioning, MQTT broker, Device twin/shadow, Telemetry ingestion, Stream processing, Command and control, OTA update service, Fleet dashboard, Certificate management. DATA STORAGE ARCHITECTURE EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES Time-series database for telemetry; document store for device twins and registry; data lake for long-term analytics and ML; object storage for firmware. Every architecture in this handbook optimizes some quality attributes by sacrificing others. Selection is a structured exercise: translate business needs into measurable quality attributes, filter by constraints, compare candidates through explicit trade-offs, and record the decision. Keep them short, immutable once accepted, and supersede rather than edit. ADR-014: Use a modular monolith with Kafka-based integration for the Order Platform Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Deciders: Platform architect, Order team lead, SRE lead Context: One team of 8 engineers; domain boundaries (Orders, Payments, Catalog) still evolving; peak 300 orders/s; SLO 99.9%; two engineers on call; need to integrate with a legacy ERP and a payment gateway. Time-to-market target: 4 months. Decision: Build one deployable with three modules, each owning a schema and exposing a public API. Publish domain events to Kafka through a transactional outbox for the ERP and analytics consumers. Defer microservices. Options: 1. Microservices from day one - rejected: ops load and boundary uncertainty 2. Layered monolith - rejected: boundary erosion, hard to split later 3. Modular monolith + outbox - chosen Consequences: (+) Local ACID transactions; one pipeline; fast delivery; clean path to extraction. (+) ERP/analytics decoupled via events without distributed transactions. (-) Single scale and release unit; module boundaries need ArchUnit enforcement. (-) Kafka and the outbox relay add operational surface. Revisit when: team > 3 squads, or any module needs independent scaling or a distinct SLO, or release contention exceeds 2 blocked merges/week. Review date: 2027-05-01. ADR practice Store ADRs in the repository next to the code (docs/adr/NNN-title.md) and review them like code. One decision per record; link superseded records instead of rewriting history. Include rejected options and the reason; this prevents re-litigating the same debate. Add explicit revisit triggers and a review date so decisions do not become dogma.

Validate each against measurable requirements, team capability and an ADR before committing. Quick revision notes Part I — Fundamental Monolith: one deployable. Modular monolith: one deployable with enforced boundaries. Microservices: many deployables owning their data. Distributed monolith is a diagnosis, not a design: distributed cost with monolithic coupling. Layered is a code style; three-tier is a deployment topology. EDA decouples via events; serverless removes server management; P2P removes the center. Part II — Domain-centric Clean, Hexagonal and Onion share one rule: dependencies point inward to the domain. DDD gives boundaries (bounded contexts) and tactical patterns (aggregates, events). Vertical slices optimize change per feature; screaming architecture reveals intent. Microkernel: tiny core, everything else a module. Plug-in: complete host with extension points. BFF: one backend per client experience; micro-frontends: independent UI deployables. Part III — Styles and communication Event = fact (past tense), command = request. Pub/sub fans out facts; queues distribute work. CQRS splits read/write models; Event Sourcing stores history; they are independent. Saga replaces distributed ACID with compensations; orchestrate complex flows, choreograph simple ones. Batch for throughput, stream for latency; Lambda = two paths, Kappa = one path with replay. Shared-nothing and space-based architectures exist to remove shared bottlenecks. Part IV — Presentation MVC → MVP → MVVM → MVI: progressively more explicit state flow. Flux and Redux formalize unidirectional flow: action → reducer → store → view. Components: props down, events up. Part V — Microservices and distributed Gateway = north–south; mesh = east–west; sidecar and ambassador are co-located helpers. Database per service; share via APIs and events; compose reads with API composition or CQRS. 2PC blocks; sagas and outbox keep services available. Multi-tenancy and cells trade cost against isolation and blast radius. Active-active = all sites live; active-passive = one live, one standby. Part VI — Data Lake = cheap raw; warehouse = modeled and fast; lakehouse = ACID tables on lake storage. Medallion layers: Bronze raw, Silver cleansed, Gold business-ready. ETL transforms before load; ELT after load. Mesh is organizational, fabric is metadata-driven. Cache hierarchy: browser → CDN → gateway → app → distributed → database. Part VII — Cloud-native Containers package; Kubernetes orchestrates; serverless abstracts servers. HA removes single points of failure; fault tolerance contains failures; DR recovers from loss (RPO/RTO). Multi-cloud costs a lot, multi-region on one cloud is usually enough; edge brings compute to the data. Part VIII — Specialized Rule-based: facts + rules + engine. Interpreter: parse then evaluate a DSL. Reflection: inspect and change behavior at runtime. Primary–replica: one writer; leader–follower: consensus-elected leader. Reactive: non-blocking with backpressure. Actor: private state + messages + supervision.
